ocar.opportunity: Connectomics is now essential for studying brain function, but most groups cannot afford the imaging time, storage, and analysis that full synaptic volumes require.
ocar.challenge: Comparative circuit work across species needs both a global map of projections and local synaptic detail, and those two resolutions pull in opposite directions on cost and throughput.
ocar.action: Gillet and colleagues built a multi-resolution imaging, processing, and analysis pipeline with standardized volume-EM preparation, acquisition, and alignment, combined with µCT trimming, automatic segmentation, synapse detection, CATMAID skeleton tracing, and CAVE proofreading.
ocar.resolution: Applied to the central complex of six insect species, the pipeline yielded cellular-resolution global projectomes (40–50 nm) with embedded local connectomes of key compartments at synaptic resolution (8–12 nm). Reconstructing head-direction cells across all six species showed conserved cell types, numbers, and projection patterns plus circuit-level specializations.
ocar.future_work: A natural next step is to test whether the same modest-resource workflow extends beyond the central complex to other neuropils and a wider set of insect species.

summaries.beginner: Mapping insect brains is usually too expensive for small labs. This team shows a cheaper way to image the same brain at two zoom levels, and they find that a navigation circuit looks largely the same across six insect species, with some local tweaks.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), this study presents an imaging, processing, and analysis pipeline for multi-resolution volume EM and circuit reconstruction, aimed at groups with modest resources. Applied to the central complex of six insect species, it produced global projectomes at 40–50 nm with embedded local connectomes at 8–12 nm, using CATMAID tracing and CAVE proofreading alongside automated segmentation and synapse detection. Reconstructing head-direction cells across species revealed conservation of cell types, cell numbers, and projection patterns, together with circuit-level specializations. The authors argue that the workflow makes comparative connectomics accessible beyond large consortia.
summaries.advanced: The claim of “democratizing” comparative connectomics rests on a six-species central-complex case study rather than a full-brain reconstruction, so transfer to larger neuropils is untested here. Resolution bands (40–50 nm vs 8–12 nm) are stated, but the abstract does not quantify error rates, tracing completeness, or wall-clock cost. Conservation is reported for head-direction cells specifically; other cell classes may not follow the same pattern. The pipeline combines new protocols with existing tools (CATMAID, CAVE), so novelty is in integration and multi-resolution strategy more than in a single algorithm.

plain_language_summary: Mapping insect brains is usually too expensive for small labs. This team shows a cheaper way to image the same brain at two zoom levels, and they find that a navigation circuit looks largely the same across six insect species, with some local tweaks.

ocar.opportunity: Reliable synapse labels are the supervision that automated connectomics needs, but human judgments on subtle 3D cues are noisy and hard to audit.
ocar.challenge: Volumetric EM synapses yield variable rater decisions, so crowdsourced labels can disagree even after training, and raw agreement scores hide residual ambiguity.
ocar.action: Lee and colleagues defined a standardized proofreading protocol with operational criteria, machine-learning candidate generation, two-stage annotator calibration, and Dawid–Skene aggregation of multi-rater labels with calibrated uncertainty, tested in two larval Drosophila volumes at 8×8×8 nm.
ocar.resolution: After calibration, each of four annotators improved versus the expert (McNemar p < 0.05), Dawid–Skene–expert agreement rose, and posterior entropy fell for true positives and negatives. Chance-corrected agreement (Krippendorff’s α) improved only modestly and in a dataset-dependent way.
ocar.future_work: The protocol still needs to be stress-tested on other volumes and synapse classes, because chance-corrected agreement gains were modest and dataset-dependent.

summaries.beginner: People often disagree about whether a tiny blob in a brain image is a synapse. This team trains raters, combines their votes with a statistical model, and reports how sure the group is, so the labels can be used more honestly.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), this study presents a standardized synapse-proofreading protocol for EM connectomics that pairs explicit criteria with model-proposed candidates and two-stage annotator calibration. In two larval Drosophila volumes imaged at 8×8×8 nm, five raters (one expert plus four calibrated annotators) labeled candidates, and judgments were aggregated with a Dawid–Skene model. Post-calibration accuracy versus the expert improved for all raters (McNemar p < 0.05), consensus became more decisive, and residual uncertainty is reported rather than hidden. The authors frame the output as auditable supervision for training and evaluation at scale.
summaries.advanced: Gains in chance-corrected agreement were modest and dataset-dependent, so the protocol does not claim to eliminate rater noise. Evaluation is against a single expert rather than an independent gold standard, and both volumes are larval Drosophila at one voxel size. The abstract does not report how the method behaves on adult fly or mammalian synapses. Making uncertainty explicit is the distinctive claim; users should treat DS posteriors as calibrated consensus, not as ground truth.

plain_language_summary: People often disagree about whether a tiny blob in a brain image is a synapse. This team trains raters, combines their votes with a statistical model, and reports how sure the group is, so the labels can be used more honestly.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomics volumes are now so large and heterogeneous that dataset-specific retraining and dense manual annotation cannot keep up.
ocar.challenge: Generic EM foundation models are not tailored to connectomics, where membrane boundaries and synaptic ultrastructure must be preserved to avoid topological and connectivity errors.
ocar.action: Abir and colleagues introduce ConnectoFM, pretrained with masked image modeling and contrastive alignment on 1.7 million unlabeled EM images from six species and 25 subdomains, then transfer frozen features with lightweight decoder heads to binary segmentation, multiclass cell typing, and instance segmentation.
ocar.resolution: Across 29 datasets, ConnectoFM outperformed existing EM foundation models and from-scratch task-specific methods. With 10% labeled data it surpassed baselines trained on a 100% annotation budget, with especially pronounced gains on membranes, mitochondria, vesicles, postsynaptic densities, and synapses.
ocar.future_work: Extending the same pretrained features to fully 3D volumetric segmentation at connectome scale, and testing whether gains hold on acquisition domains outside the 25-subdomain corpus, is the obvious next test.

summaries.beginner: Computers that trace neurons from electron-microscope pictures usually have to be retrained for every new dataset. This team pretrains one model on a huge mix of unlabeled brain images and shows it can learn new tracing jobs with far fewer hand-drawn labels.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), this study presents ConnectoFM, described as a foundation model for connectomics, pretrained on 1.7 million unlabeled EM images from six species and 25 subdomains using masked image modeling plus contrastive alignment. Frozen features with light decoder heads are transferred to binary segmentation, multiclass cell typing, and instance segmentation. Across 29 datasets the model outperforms existing EM foundation models and from-scratch specialists, and with 10% labels it beats baselines trained on 100% of the annotation budget. Gains are emphasized for membranes, mitochondria, vesicles, postsynaptic densities, and synapses.
summaries.advanced: The abstract reports consistent outperformance and a striking 10%-vs-100% label result, but does not name the competing foundation models or give per-dataset scores here. Pretraining spans six species and 25 subdomains; generalization beyond that mix is asserted via the 29-dataset suite rather than a fully held-out species. Extension to 3D volumetric segmentation is described as further evidence, not as a completed whole-brain reconstruction. Users should treat “first foundation model for connectomics” as an authorship claim pending independent benchmarks.

plain_language_summary: Computers that trace neurons from electron-microscope pictures usually have to be retrained for every new dataset. This team pretrains one model on a huge mix of unlabeled brain images and shows it can learn new tracing jobs with far fewer hand-drawn labels.

ocar.opportunity: Generative models of cortical wiring usually start from measured features such as morphology, molecular identity, and location, so they can only use what we already know how to measure.
ocar.challenge: Those assumed features may miss the variables that actually predict synapses, and detailed cell-type catalogs are incomplete even in well-studied cortex.
ocar.action: Richter and Schneidman jointly learn low-dimensional neuronal embeddings and wiring rules that predict synapses in a column of mouse primary visual cortex, without feeding in a full cell-type taxonomy.
ocar.resolution: Embedding-based models predicted individual synapses, degrees, and motif statistics better than standard generative models that depend on detailed cell-type classifications, using only a handful of embedding dimensions and wiring rules. The embeddings recovered cortical depth, cell type, and dendritic morphology, suggesting a parsimonious cortical wiring logic.
ocar.future_work: The framework is offered as exportable; the next test is whether similarly compact embeddings recover wiring rules in other cortical areas and species.

summaries.beginner: Instead of starting from known cell labels, this study lets a model invent a compact description of each neuron and the simple rules that wire them together in mouse visual cortex. The invented description still tracks things biologists care about, such as depth and cell type.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), this study presents a representational-learning approach to the circuitry of a mouse primary visual cortex column. The model jointly learns low-dimensional embeddings of neurons and wiring rules that predict synaptic connectivity. These embedding-based models accurately predict individual synapses, connectivity degrees, and network-motif statistics, outperforming standard generative models that rely on detailed cell-type classifications, while using only a handful of dimensions and rules. The learned features recapitulate cortical depth, cell type, and dendritic morphology.
summaries.advanced: Outperformance is stated relative to generative models that depend on detailed cell-type classifications; the abstract does not report numerical accuracies. Success on one V1 column does not establish that cortical connectivity is universally low-dimensional. Interpretability is claimed because embeddings recover known axes (depth, type, dendrite shape), which could also mean the model rediscovered those axes rather than a deeper unknown code. Motif statistics are predicted, but the abstract does not specify which motifs.

plain_language_summary: Instead of starting from known cell labels, this study lets a model invent a compact description of each neuron and the simple rules that wire them together in mouse visual cortex. The invented description still tracks things biologists care about, such as depth and cell type.

ocar.opportunity: Complete larval and adult Drosophila connectomes now make it possible to ask how an entire brain rewires across metamorphosis, not just how a few identified neurons change.
ocar.challenge: Larval and adult networks differ in density, cell composition, and which neurons sit at the structural core, so comparing them requires matched network statistics rather than a neuron-by-neuron map.
ocar.action: Yadav, Shinde, and Singh compared degree distributions, structural cores, and rich-club organization of Drosophila melanogaster brain networks at larval versus adult stages.
ocar.resolution: The denser larval network fitted a Weibull degree distribution; the sparser adult network was closer to scale-free. The larval structural core sat in mushroom-body neurons with a rich-club; the adult core shifted to antennal-lobe neurons, consistent with reduced mushroom-body centrality after metamorphosis.
ocar.future_work: Linking these graph-level shifts to identified cell types and behaviors across metamorphosis would test whether the core relocation is a computational change or mainly a density-and-centrality artifact.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly brains are rewired as the animal grows from larva to adult. This paper compares the two wiring diagrams and finds that the adult network is sparser and more hub-like, and that the most central cells change from a learning center to an odor center.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Network Neuroscience (2025), this study presents a comparative graph analysis of larval versus adult Drosophila melanogaster brain networks. The larval degree distribution fitted a Weibull model, whereas the sparser adult network followed a power-law pattern, with the out-degree exponent in the scale-free regime and the in-degree exponent close to it. The larval structural core comprised mushroom-body neurons and formed a rich club; the adult core comprised antennal-lobe neurons, and only the larva showed rich-club organization. The authors attribute the core shift to reduced mushroom-body centrality after metamorphosis.
summaries.advanced: Scale-free and Weibull fits are model comparisons on observed degree sequences; the abstract does not report goodness-of-fit statistics or robustness to synapse-thresholding. The adult network is described as sparser, so some topological differences could follow from density alone. Mapping “mushroom body” versus “antennal lobe” cores depends on how neurons are assigned to regions in each connectome. The study is comparative across two life stages of one species, not a developmental time series of many individuals.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly brains are rewired as the animal grows from larva to adult. This paper compares the two wiring diagrams and finds that the adult network is sparser and more hub-like, and that the most central cells change from a learning center to an odor center.

ocar.opportunity: A synapse-level adult fly connectome specifies possible routes for sensory signals, but not how those routes would unfold as dynamic cascades.
ocar.challenge: Tracing modality-specific flow, overlap among senses, and neuron roles from anatomy alone is underdetermined without an explicit spreading process.
ocar.action: Betzel and colleagues simulated sensory propagation on the adult Drosophila connectome with a network spreading model, then added cooperative and competitive dynamics and clustered neurons by their response profiles across simulations.
ocar.resolution: The model produced modality-specific cascades, overlap zones of multi-pathway activation, and a data-driven neuron taxonomy grounded in both structure and dynamics.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the taxonomy as a source of hypotheses for experimental validation, so the next step is to test predicted cascade overlap and cell classes against physiological recordings.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram shows which cells touch, not how a signal would actually travel. This team runs simple spreading simulations on the fly brain map to guess which cells light up together for different senses.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2025), this study presents a network spreading model of sensory signal flow on the adult Drosophila connectome. The authors trace modality-specific cascades, quantify neurons activated by multiple sensory pathways, and extend the model with cooperative and competitive dynamics for multisensory integration. Neurons are then classified by dynamical response profiles across simulations, yielding a taxonomy tied to both wiring and dynamics. The work is framed as generating experimentally testable hypotheses about organizing principles of neural computation.
summaries.advanced: The spreading model is intentionally simple and linear-style; the abstract does not claim biophysical synapses or measured delays. Cooperative and competitive extensions are simulated scenarios, not fitted to physiology in this report. The resulting taxonomy is data-driven within the simulation suite, so it may not match molecular or morphological cell types. Validation against recordings is proposed, not performed here.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram shows which cells touch, not how a signal would actually travel. This team runs simple spreading simulations on the fly brain map to guess which cells light up together for different senses.

ocar.opportunity: Large, shared EM connectomes are now being proofread and annotated by many users at once, so the community needs infrastructure that keeps reconstructions and analyses in sync.
ocar.challenge: Every proofreading edit can relabel millions of voxels and thousands of synapses, yet analysts still need immediate, reproducible queries while the dataset is changing.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald and colleagues built CAVE, a Connectome Annotation Versioning Engine that distributes proofreading with continuous versioning and stores annotations by location so they can be reassigned to segments at arbitrary time points.
ocar.resolution: CAVE supports schematized, extensible annotation types and fast analysis queries on up-to-petascale (~1 mm³) datasets while proofreading continues. It is already used for many connectomics datasets, including the largest then available.
ocar.future_work: As volumes grow beyond a cubic millimeter, the same location-based versioning model will need to keep query latency acceptable for still-larger concurrent communities.

summaries.beginner: When many people correct a giant brain map at once, cell names and synapse lists keep changing. CAVE is software that versions those edits so scientists can still run analyses and get the same answer later.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Methods (2025), this study presents CAVE, infrastructure for concurrent proofreading and reproducible analysis of up-to-petascale (~1 mm³) EM connectomes. A distributed proofreading system continuously versions large reconstructions, and annotations are defined by locations so they can be quickly assigned to the current segment. That design enables analysis queries at arbitrary time points and supports new, schematized annotation types. The authors report that CAVE is already used across many datasets, including the largest available to date.
summaries.advanced: CAVE is infrastructure rather than a new segmentation algorithm; its value depends on adoption and operational scale, which the abstract asserts but does not benchmark with latency numbers. The ~1 mm³ figure is the targeted operating regime, not a claim that every hosted dataset is that large. Location-based annotations assume that spatial coordinates remain meaningful across alignment versions. The MICrONS mouse dataset is among the streams tagged for this paper, but the abstract describes a multi-dataset system rather than a single-volume result.

plain_language_summary: When many people correct a giant brain map at once, cell names and synapse lists keep changing. CAVE is software that versions those edits so scientists can still run analyses and get the same answer later.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical cell types are well described anatomically and molecularly, but the synaptic rules that place each inhibitory type into the circuit have been hard to map at scale.
ocar.challenge: Connectivity principles at the resolution of distinct cell types require dense, millimeter-scale EM and a way to classify both inhibitory and excitatory neurons from structure.
ocar.action: Schneider-Mizell and colleagues used volumetric EM to map all inhibitory neurons among 1,352 densely segmented cells spanning all layers of mouse visual cortex, reconstructing more than 70,000 inhibitory synapses, and classified cells from dendritic compartment targeting and whole-cell synaptic-input maps.
ocar.resolution: They identified a disinhibitory specialist that targets basket cells, widespread interneuron specificity for spatially intermingled excitatory subpopulations, and “motif groups” that collectively innervate perisomatic and dendritic compartments of the same excitatory targets.
ocar.future_work: The census is positioned as a foundation for linking multimodal neuronal atlases to the cortical wiring diagram, so aligning these EM types with molecular atlases is the immediate follow-on.

summaries.beginner: Inhibitory cells in the cortex come in many kinds, but it has been unclear exactly whom each kind talks to. This team mapped inhibition across a column of mouse visual cortex and found that inhibitory cells are choosier than a random mix would suggest.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2025), this study presents a synaptic-resolution census of inhibition across a densely segmented population of 1,352 cells spanning all layers of mouse visual cortex, with more than 70,000 synapses. Inhibitory neurons were classified by dendritic-compartment targeting, and excitatory neurons by dendritic reconstructions plus whole-cell synaptic-input maps. Single-cell connectivity revealed a disinhibitory specialist targeting basket cells, widespread targeting specificity among intermingled excitatory subpopulations, and motif groups that jointly innervate soma and dendrites of the same excitatory cells. The authors argue these are organizing principles for cortical inhibition.
summaries.advanced: The census covers one visual-cortex column in one animal; generality across areas and individuals is not shown here. Classification is structural, inspired by classical neuroanatomy, not molecular. “Widespread specificity” is a qualitative summary of many interneurons, not a single selectivity index. The companion preprint (2023) reports the same cell and synapse counts, indicating this Nature paper is the journal version of that census rather than an expanded volume.

plain_language_summary: Inhibitory cells in the cortex come in many kinds, but it has been unclear exactly whom each kind talks to. This team mapped inhibition across a column of mouse visual cortex and found that inhibitory cells are choosier than a random mix would suggest.

ocar.opportunity: Millimeter-scale EM volumes now yield dense cellular meshes, but turning those meshes into proofread neurons and usable morphological features still takes heavy custom engineering.
ocar.challenge: Automated segmentation remains riddled with merge and split errors, and extracting spines, branches, and axonal–dendritic relations from elaborate 3D meshes is fragmented across tools.
ocar.action: Celii and colleagues introduce NEURD (Neural Decomposition), which decomposes meshed neurons into compact, annotated graphs and uses those graphs to automate proofreading of merge errors, cell classification, spine detection, and axonal–dendritic proximity features.
ocar.resolution: The package, built on existing open-source mesh software, is reported to reach state-of-the-art automated merge-error proofreading and to make morphology and connectivity analyses more accessible on massive EM datasets.
ocar.future_work: Split-error correction and fully automated, dataset-agnostic proofreading remain open; applying NEURD graphs uniformly across species and labs would test how far the feature set transfers.

summaries.beginner: Computers can now outline cells in huge electron-microscope volumes, but the outlines still have mistakes and are hard to measure. NEURD turns each cell’s 3D shape into a simpler labeled graph so corrections and measurements can be automated.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2025), this study presents NEURD, software that decomposes neuronal meshes from high-resolution EM volumes into feature-rich graph representations. Those graphs are used to automate merge-error proofreading, cell classification, spine detection, axonal–dendritic proximities, and related annotations. The authors report state-of-the-art automated proofreading of merge errors and argue that the representation unlocks downstream morphological and connectivity analyses. The work is positioned as making millimetre-scale EM connectomes more accessible to neuroscience researchers.
summaries.advanced: NEURD targets merge errors specifically; split errors are acknowledged as remaining work for proofreading pipelines generally. “State-of-the-art” is claimed in the abstract without numerical benchmarks here. The method operates on already-meshed, already-segmented neurons, so it inherits upstream segmentation failures. Feature extraction quality will depend on mesh fidelity, which varies across EM modalities and labs.

plain_language_summary: Computers can now outline cells in huge electron-microscope volumes, but the outlines still have mistakes and are hard to measure. NEURD turns each cell’s 3D shape into a simpler labeled graph so corrections and measurements can be automated.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic-resolution connectomics aims to map how evolution and experience implement circuits, but until recently accessible volumes were limited to specialized miniature neuropils.
ocar.challenge: Scaling 3D EM and analysis from about 100 µm³ to about 1 mm³ still leaves centimetre-scale targets—local human cortex, whole small reptiles or rodents, and ultimately a whole mouse brain—out of reach, with remaining bottlenecks in preparation, sectioning or ablation, imaging, and AI reconstruction.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter reviews two decades of methodological advances in tissue preparation, ablation or sectioning, imaging, and AI-based 3D analysis that expanded connectomically accessible synaptic-resolution volumes by a factor of about 1,000.
ocar.resolution: The field can now move beyond miniature circuits to a large range of local mouse neuropil, including cortical grey matter. The same advances also enable multifold mapping of smaller circuits for connectomic screening of experience, age, and pathology.
ocar.future_work: Resolving local circuits of larger brains, including human, and whole-brain synaptic connectomes of small reptiles, rodents, birds, and non-human primates is identified as the next major target, with a whole adult mouse brain as a particular remaining challenge.

summaries.beginner: Scientists can now map tiny pieces of brain at the level of individual connections, about a thousand times larger than twenty years ago. This review explains what that makes possible next—and why a whole mouse brain at that detail is still a huge leap.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2025), this review surveys synaptic-resolution connectomics and the methods that expanded accessible volumes from about 100 µm³ to about 1 mm³. Helmstaedter argues the field can now map a wide range of local mouse neuropil, including cortical grey matter, rather than only specialized miniature circuits. He discusses remaining challenges for centimetre-scale targets such as a whole adult mouse brain, and emphasizes that the same methods now allow repeated mapping of smaller circuits. That “connectomic screening” could address interactions among evolutionary determinism, experience, behavior, aging, and pathology.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective review, not a new dataset; volume factors (1,000-fold; 100 µm³ to 1 mm³) are field-level estimates. Claims about readiness for local mouse cortex versus unreadiness for whole mouse brain are strategic, not accompanied by a single benchmark table here. “Connectomic screening” is a proposed use of smaller multifold maps, contingent on throughput and biological perturbation designs not specified in the abstract. Mouse is the organism tag, but the review’s horizon includes human and other vertebrates.

plain_language_summary: Scientists can now map tiny pieces of brain at the level of individual connections, about a thousand times larger than twenty years ago. This review explains what that makes possible next—and why a whole mouse brain at that detail is still a huge leap.

ocar.opportunity: Most odors in Drosophila are encoded combinatorially across glomeruli, but some ecologically special odors use a single specialized pathway—and it has been unclear how those two computational styles differ at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: Comparing dense glomerular connectomes requires targeting identified glomeruli in volume EM and then scoring innervation, synapse composition, and motifs across cell classes.
ocar.action: Gruber and colleagues laser-branded glomeruli of interest and used FIB-SEM to densely reconstruct a broadly tuned glomerulus (DL5) and a narrowly tuned glomerulus (DA2), then compared them with a previously mapped narrow glomerulus (VA1v).
ocar.resolution: Narrow glomeruli shared putative generic features: higher fiber and synapse density, less OSN lateralization, stronger OSN axo-axonic connections, dendro-dendritic connections among many uPNs, and less presynaptic input onto OSN axons. The single DL5 uPN also contained many autapses linking distant dendritic regions.
ocar.future_work: Whether the same motifs distinguish other specialist versus combinatorial glomeruli, and whether autapses in DL5 are typical of uniglomerular PNs with a single dendrite tree, remains to be tested.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies smell some odors with many glomeruli at once and other special odors with just one. This paper compares the wiring inside one “generalist” and one “specialist” glomerulus and lists connection patterns that may go with each job.
summaries.intermediate: This 2025 eLife/bioRxiv study uses laser branding plus FIB-SEM to reconstruct Drosophila glomeruli DL5 (broadly tuned) and DA2 (narrowly tuned) and compares them with previously mapped VA1v. The authors report differences in innervation, synaptic composition, and circuit diagrams among olfactory sensory neurons, uniglomerular projection neurons, and multiglomerular neurons. Narrow glomeruli showed higher neuronal-fiber and synapse density, lower OSN lateralization, stronger OSN axo-axonic synapses, uPN dendro-dendritic coupling, and less presynaptic input on OSN axons. DL5’s single uPN also contained substantial autapses spanning its dendritic tree.
summaries.advanced: Generic features of narrow glomeruli are inferred from DA2 plus one previously mapped glomerulus (VA1v), a small n for a typology. DL5 autapses are a striking observation from one uniglomerular PN and should not be assumed for all combinatorial glomeruli. Laser branding enables targeting but could, in principle, affect ultrastructure; the abstract does not discuss that risk. Motifs are anatomical; computational “demands” are interpreted from known glomerular tuning, not measured here in the same animals.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies smell some odors with many glomeruli at once and other special odors with just one. This paper compares the wiring inside one “generalist” and one “specialist” glomerulus and lists connection patterns that may go with each job.

ocar.opportunity: Body-wide motor control is coordinated by synaptic circuits, but cellular-level whole-body wiring of a segmented animal has been largely unknown.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing every neuronal and non-neuronal cell in a whole-body EM volume, then classifying types and tracing left–right, intersegmental, and effector pathways, is a large annotation problem.
ocar.action: Verasztó and colleagues reconstructed and annotated over 9,000 cells in a serial EM volume of a Platynereis dumerilii larva, classifying differentiated cells into 202 neuronal and 92 non-neuronal types and analyzing modularity, multisensory integration, and motor circuits.
ocar.resolution: They report segment-specific types (heteromery) alongside serially homologous types across head, trunk, and pygidium, plus descending and ascending pathways, peptidergic circuits, and a multimodal mechanosensory girdle, providing a basis for studying whole-body coordination in a segmented animal.
ocar.future_work: Physiological tests of the reconstructed ciliary, gland, pigment, and muscle pathways are needed to show which of the mapped routes actually drive larval behavior.

summaries.beginner: This team mapped the cells and connections of an entire young marine worm, not just its brain. The map shows how segments share cell types and how senses can reach muscles, cilia, and glands across the body.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2025), this study presents a whole-body synaptic connectome of a segmented Platynereis dumerilii larva. The authors reconstructed and annotated over 9,000 neuronal and non-neuronal cells, classifying differentiated cells into 202 neuronal and 92 non-neuronal types. Analyses cover modularity, multisensory integration, left–right and intersegmental connectivity, and motor circuits for ciliated cells, glands, pigment cells, and muscles. Segment-specific types demonstrate heteromery, while repeated types across head, trunk, and pygidium suggest serial homology of all segmental regions.
summaries.advanced: Cell-type counts (202 neuronal, 92 non-neuronal) are annotation products of one larva; stereotypy across individuals is not reported here. “Over 9,000” cells includes non-neuronal cells, so this is not a 9,000-neuron brain. Heteromery versus serial homology is a dual finding that depends on type definitions. A related 2020 preprint described a three-segmented larva with smaller reconstructed counts, so readers should treat this 2025 report as a later, larger whole-body effort rather than the same dataset restated.

plain_language_summary: This team mapped the cells and connections of an entire young marine worm, not just its brain. The map shows how segments share cell types and how senses can reach muscles, cilia, and glands across the body.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding human brain function at the level of synapses has been limited by the lack of a large, high-quality ultrastructural sample of normal-adjacent human cortex.
ocar.challenge: Human tissue is rarely biopsied except near pathology; organoids lack cortical layering; and reconstructing a cubic millimeter at nanoscale resolution is a petascale imaging and proofreading problem.
ocar.action: Shapson-Coe and colleagues imaged a 1 mm³ piece of human temporal cortex, removed during surgery to access an epileptic focus, with high-throughput serial-section EM and computationally reconstructed cells, vessels, and synapses, releasing the 1.4-petabyte H01 resource with analysis tools.
ocar.resolution: The volume contains about 57,000 cells, about 230 mm of blood vessels, and about 150 million synapses. Glia outnumbered neurons 2:1, oligodendrocytes were the most common cell, deep-layer excitatory neurons could be classified by dendritic orientation, and rare powerful axonal inputs of up to 50 synapses sat among thousands of weak connections per neuron.
ocar.future_work: The authors present H01 as a public resource for further study of normal and disordered human circuits; independent proofreading and comparison to additional patients are needed before treating rare motifs as human universals.

summaries.beginner: Researchers reconstructed a cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex at very high detail and posted the data for anyone to explore. They found more support cells than neurons, and a few unusually strong connections mixed in with many weak ones.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2024), this study presents a nanoscale reconstruction of 1 mm³ of human temporal cortex obtained during surgery to reach an underlying epileptic focus. Serial-section EM produced 1.4 petabytes of data containing about 57,000 cells, about 230 mm of blood vessels, and about 150 million synapses. Analysis found glia outnumbering neurons 2:1, oligodendrocytes as the most common cell, a previously unrecognized class of directionally oriented deep-layer neurons, and rare multi-synaptic axonal inputs of up to 50 synapses. All data and tools are shared as the H01 resource.
summaries.advanced: Tissue is surgical access-path cortex from a patient with epilepsy, so “normal human cortex” is an approximation. A companion 2021 preprint reported 57,216 cells and 133.7 million synapses in a 1 mm³ temporal sample; this Science article’s ~150 million synapses and ~57,000 cells should be read as the published resource counts, not mixed with the preprint’s synapse total. Up-to-50-synapse inputs are described as rare; prevalence across individuals is unknown. Automated reconstruction is incomplete, and the authors explicitly invite community proofreading.

plain_language_summary: Researchers reconstructed a cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex at very high detail and posted the data for anyone to explore. They found more support cells than neurons, and a few unusually strong connections mixed in with many weak ones.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric reconstructions now yield neuron-level connectomes in fly, mouse, and human, creating a chance to test whether those networks share simple physical and topological organizing rules.
ocar.challenge: Spatial embedding and degree sequence each explain part of the structure, but neither constraint alone recovers the other: positions look distance-optimal, yet space misses the broad degree distribution, and degrees miss geometry.
ocar.action: Salova and Kovács built contactomes (neurons in physical contact) alongside connectomes and fitted scalable maximum-entropy models that combine spatial or contact constraints with topological constraints.
ocar.resolution: Joint models captured biological and network features beyond the inputs, including synaptic weights and graphlet statistics, pointing to shared organizing principles across the three organisms.
ocar.future_work: Testing whether the same joint spatial–topological ensemble predicts held-out volumes or developmental stages would show if the principles are generative rather than descriptive of current snapshots.

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring is shaped both by which cells sit near each other and by how many partners each cell has. This paper shows you need both kinds of rules to copy the structure of fly, mouse, and human connection maps.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Network Neuroscience (2024), this study models fruit-fly, mouse, and human neural connectomes in physical context by constructing contactomes of neurons in contact. Neuron positions are highly optimal in distance to neighbors, but spatial constraints alone miss topology including the broad degree distribution, while the degree sequence alone misses spatial structure. Scalable maximum-entropy models combining both constraint types generate networks that also capture synaptic weights and graphlet statistics. The authors interpret this as a shared, simple set of organizing principles across organisms.
summaries.advanced: “Shared principles” are inferred from successful joint maximum-entropy fits, not from a single universal parameter set reported here. Contactomes depend on morphological reconstructions and contact definitions that may differ by dataset. Predictive power “beyond the input data” for weights and graphlets is encouraging but can still reflect correlations already implicit in space and degree. Human and mouse reconstructions used here are local volumes, not whole brains, unlike the fly case.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring is shaped both by which cells sit near each other and by how many partners each cell has. This paper shows you need both kinds of rules to copy the structure of fly, mouse, and human connection maps.

ocar.opportunity: In insects the neck connective is a physical and informational bottleneck between brain and ventral nerve cord, so a complete account of descending and ascending neurons is needed to link sensation to action.
ocar.challenge: These neurons are split across brain and nerve-cord EM volumes and differ by sex, so they must be matched across hemispheres, datasets, and sexes and tied to genetic driver lines.
ocar.action: Stürner and colleagues integrated three EM datasets to proofread and match female Drosophila descending and ascending neurons, compared them with the male nerve cord, matched 51% of descending cell types to light-level driver lines, and classified all ascending populations.
ocar.resolution: They describe architecture, tracts, neuropil innervation, and connectivity of neck-connective neurons, including chains spanning the neck that may support motor sequences, and they fully describe sexually dimorphic DN and AN populations implicated in ovipositor extrusion, male courtship, and song.
ocar.future_work: Functional tests of the identified dimorphic circuits, and completing driver-line matches beyond the reported 51% of DN types, would close the loop from EM identity to behavior.

summaries.beginner: Messages between a fly’s brain and its body travel through a narrow neck. This team finished mapping those up and down neurons in a female fly, compared them with a male, and tied many types to genetic tools.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), this study presents a complete connectomic description of Drosophila ascending and descending neurons in the female nervous system, integrating three EM datasets and comparing them with the male nerve cord. Proofread reconstructions were matched across hemispheres, datasets, and sexes; 51% of descending cell types were matched to light-level driver lines, and all ascending populations were classified. The authors report neck-spanning DN–AN chains and a complete account of sexually dimorphic populations, including circuits for female ovipositor extrusion (DNp13), male courtship (DNa12/aSP22), and song (AN hemilineage 08B). They frame this as the first EM-level circuit analysis spanning an adult animal’s entire central nervous system.
summaries.advanced: “Complete” refers to the ascending/descending populations after matching across three volumes, not to every neuron in brain plus VNC. Driver-line matching is 51% of DN types, so many types still lack genetic reagents in this report. Sexual dimorphism analyses depend on cross-dataset matching quality between female and male nerve cords. Behavioral roles (oviposition, courtship, song) are assigned via implicated circuits and prior literature, not new behavior experiments in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Messages between a fly’s brain and its body travel through a narrow neck. This team finished mapping those up and down neurons in a female fly, compared them with a male, and tied many types to genetic tools.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain mammalian connectomes, especially mouse, are becoming a realistic planning target, so groups need a quantitative comparison of imaging methods before organizing large projects.
ocar.challenge: Candidate methods differ in resolution, speed, and maturity, and only some can both resolve all synapses and run at a pace relevant to whole mammalian brains.
ocar.action: Collins, Huffman, and Koene quantitatively compare electron microscopy techniques and expansion light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (ExLSFM) against those dual requirements.
ocar.resolution: The paper is offered as a resource for planning whole-brain mammalian connectomics, with mouse nearer-term and human a more distant goal.
ocar.future_work: As throughput and resolution of both EM and ExLSFM continue to change, the same comparison will need updating before locking in a whole-mouse or human acquisition architecture.

summaries.beginner: Scientists want maps of entire mammal brains at the level of connections, starting with the mouse. This paper compares camera-like electron microscopes and expansion light-sheet methods to see which could finish that job.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Cell Reports Methods (2024), this study quantitatively compares imaging technologies that could support whole-brain mammalian connectomics. The authors restrict attention to methods with sufficient resolution to identify all synapses and sufficient speed to be relevant to whole mammalian brains, performing calculations on electron microscopy and expansion light-sheet fluorescence microscopy. Mouse connectomes are described as soon coming within reach, human connectomes as more distant. The analysis is framed as a planning resource rather than a new acquisition.
summaries.advanced: This is a prospective methods comparison, not an empirical bake-off on the same sample. “Could soon come within reach” for mouse is a judgment, not a demonstrated whole-brain dataset. Expansion light-sheet is included only insofar as it meets the synapse-resolution and speed cuts the authors impose. Human whole-brain synaptic imaging remains aspirational in this account.

plain_language_summary: Scientists want maps of entire mammal brains at the level of connections, starting with the mouse. This paper compares camera-like electron microscopes and expansion light-sheet methods to see which could finish that job.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding how the brain controls the body requires following circuits all the way to muscles, which in insects live in the ventral nerve cord rather than the brain.
ocar.challenge: A dense EM volume of an adult female Drosophila VNC still needs automated neuron and synapse segmentation plus an atlas of which motor neurons innervate which muscles.
ocar.action: Azevedo and colleagues applied automated tools to segment neurons and identify synapses in a female fly VNC EM dataset, and mapped leg and wing motor-neuron muscle targets with genetic driver lines and X-ray holographic nanotomography.
ocar.resolution: They report roughly 45 million synapses and 14,600 neuronal cell bodies in the fly VNC, a motor-neuron atlas, and identified circuits coordinating leg and wing movements during take-off, released with programmatic and interactive access.
ocar.future_work: Using the atlas to drive targeted physiology of take-off and walking circuits, and comparing this female VNC with the male MANC volume, would test how general the reconstructed motor modules are.

summaries.beginner: A fruit fly’s “spinal cord” contains the cells that move legs and wings. This team automatically traced that cord, matched motor neurons to muscles, and spotted circuits that help the fly take off.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2024), this study presents an automated dense reconstruction of an adult female Drosophila ventral nerve cord. The VNC contains roughly 45 million synapses and 14,600 neuronal cell bodies. Muscle targets of leg and wing motor neurons were mapped with genetic driver lines and X-ray holographic nanotomography, yielding a motor-neuron atlas used to identify circuits that coordinate leg and wing movements during take-off. Reconstructions, atlas, and access tools are released as resources for studying motor control.
summaries.advanced: Counts are for one female VNC; sexual dimorphism is not addressed in this abstract (a related male VNC connectome exists separately). Automated segmentation plus targeted motor-neuron mapping is not the same as fully proofread completeness for every neuron class. Take-off circuit identification uses the atlas and connectivity; the abstract does not report new behavioral recordings. XNH is used for muscle targeting, complementing rather than replacing EM synapses.

plain_language_summary: A fruit fly’s “spinal cord” contains the cells that move legs and wings. This team automatically traced that cord, matched motor neurons to muscles, and spotted circuits that help the fly take off.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans synaptic connectome is fully mapped, but much less is known about the causal signaling network that actually propagates activity among neurons.
ocar.challenge: Structure and function can diverge: modules, hubs, and rich clubs defined from synapses need not be the ones that dominate signal flow.
ocar.action: Dvali and colleagues compared the modular architecture of a C. elegans signal-propagation network, measured with calcium imaging and optogenetics, to anatomical wiring from electron microscopy.
ocar.resolution: Signaling modules were not aligned with anatomical module boundaries, yet the pharynx remained a separate community in both. Signaling modules were enriched for specific cell types and functions, and a signaling rich club of hub neurons only overlapped the anatomical rich club at AVEL/R.
ocar.future_work: The mismatch implies that influence in this nervous system cannot be read off degree; mapping how neuromodulation reshapes the signaling modules would be a direct next experiment.

summaries.beginner: Knowing which worm neurons are wired together is not the same as knowing which ones actually pass signals. This study measures signal spread and finds that the functional groups only partly match the wiring groups.
summaries.intermediate: Published in PRX Life (2024), this study compares the C. elegans synaptic connectome with a causal signal-propagation network from calcium imaging and optogenetics. Signaling modules do not align with anatomical module boundaries, although the pharynx is a separate community in both maps. Signaling modules are enriched for particular cell types and functions, and a rich club of signaling hubs has different membership from the anatomical rich club, overlapping only at AVEL/R. The result challenges the view that structural hubs occupy matching positions of influence in functional networks.
summaries.advanced: The signaling network is defined by the authors’ perturbation-and-imaging assay; different stimuli or timescales could regroup modules. Only the most extreme anatomical feature (pharynx) and highest-degree cells (AVEL/R) are clearly preserved, which may be a generic core-periphery effect. Rich-club comparison depends on thresholding both graphs. The abstract does not quantify how much of the signaling graph is unexplained by one- or two-hop anatomy.

plain_language_summary: Knowing which worm neurons are wired together is not the same as knowing which ones actually pass signals. This study measures signal spread and finds that the functional groups only partly match the wiring groups.

ocar.opportunity: Split-GAL4 drivers and EM connectomes make the Drosophila mushroom body accessible, but many cell types upstream and downstream still lack specific genetic access.
ocar.challenge: Without driver lines, functional tests of sensory afferents, MB-extrinsic partners, and other associated neurons stall even when the wiring is known.
ocar.action: Shuai and colleagues generated a collection of over 800 split-GAL4 and split-LexA drivers covering about 300 cell types, characterized activation phenotypes for a subset, and used associated confocal images to quantify morphological stereotypy.
ocar.resolution: They identify a sugar sensory neuron line suited to reward substitution and find that MBON08/MBON09 show striking individuality and asymmetry across animals. Together with EM maps, the collection is offered as a resource for dissecting adult associative-learning circuits.
ocar.future_work: Systematic functional use of the new lines, especially the less-stereotyped MBONs, is needed to test how individual morphological variation affects learning.

summaries.beginner: To test what each cell type does in fly learning, scientists need genetic on-switches for those cells. This paper releases hundreds of such switches and notices that one pair of output cells looks surprisingly different from fly to fly.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), this study presents a collection of over 800 split-GAL4 and split-LexA drivers covering approximately 300 Drosophila cell types, including sugar sensory neurons, putative nociceptive ascending neurons, olfactory and thermo-/hygro-sensory projection neurons, and interneurons connected with mushroom-body extrinsic neurons. Activation phenotyping identified a sugar sensory line most suitable for reward substitution. Analysis of associated confocal images showed that MBON08/MBON09 exhibit striking individuality and left–right asymmetry across animals. The resource is meant to be used with EM connectome maps for functional dissection of associative learning.
summaries.advanced: Coverage is “approximately 300 cell types” among “over 800” drivers; specificity and completeness per type are not quantified in the abstract. MBON08/09 individuality is a morphological finding from light microscopy, not a connectivity or physiological variability measurement here. Driver utility for intersectional experiments will depend on split-half expression not detailed in the abstract. Confocal plus EM is the intended combination; this paper itself is a genetic/anatomy resource, not a new connectome.

plain_language_summary: To test what each cell type does in fly learning, scientists need genetic on-switches for those cells. This paper releases hundreds of such switches and notices that one pair of output cells looks surprisingly different from fly to fly.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic neuron segmentation is essential for connectome reconstruction, but standard image CNNs only see local shape context.
ocar.challenge: Merge and split errors and cell-type identity often depend on global neuron geometry that voxel-wise networks do not represent well.
ocar.action: Troidl and colleagues introduce a point affinity transformer that embeds a (multi-)neuron point cloud into a fixed-length feature set from which any point-pair affinity can be decoded, supporting clustering for automatic proofreading and mapping features into a contrastive space for type classification.
ocar.resolution: On three benchmark datasets from state-of-the-art connectomes, the method outperformed point transformers, graph neural networks, and unsupervised clustering baselines on segmentation-error correction and neuron-type classification.
ocar.future_work: Scaling the transformer from benchmark fragments to whole-brain point clouds, and testing whether affinities transfer across EM labs, would show if global shape reasoning can replace a large share of human proofreading.

summaries.beginner: Computers that trace neurons usually look at small patches of the image. This method looks at the whole sketched shape of a cell as a cloud of points, which helps it fix tracing mistakes and guess the cell’s type.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), this study presents a point affinity transformer for global neuron-shape reasoning in connectomics. A (multi-)neuron point cloud is embedded into a fixed-length feature set from which point-pair affinities can be decoded, enabling clustering for automatic proofreading. The same features map into a contrastive space used for neuron-type classification with a simple classifier. Evaluated on three benchmarks derived from state-of-the-art connectomes, the approach outperformed point transformers, graph neural networks, and unsupervised clustering baselines.
summaries.advanced: Outperformance is reported without numeric scores in the abstract. Benchmarks are derived from existing connectomes, so they may not capture the full error distribution of raw automated segmentation. The method assumes a point-cloud representation of neurons, which already requires a skeleton or mesh step. Classification via a mapped contrastive space is shown to be easy once features exist; the hard part remains affinity quality on rare morphologies.

plain_language_summary: Computers that trace neurons usually look at small patches of the image. This method looks at the whole sketched shape of a cell as a cloud of points, which helps it fix tracing mistakes and guess the cell’s type.

ocar.opportunity: Neuron-resolution connectomes with cell-type annotations, such as the larval Drosophila brain, finally let researchers test whether graph communities correspond to biological cell classes.
ocar.challenge: Standard community detection is single-scale and unweighted; relating multi-level blocks to function, cell type, and communication paths is harder.
ocar.action: Betzel, Puxeddu, and Seguin applied a hierarchical weighted stochastic blockmodel to a published larval Drosophila connectome and compared blocks to functional and cell-type maps, then examined assortativity, rich-club membership, and polysynaptic trajectories.
ocar.resolution: Communities largely partitioned neurons by function and cell type and mostly interacted assortatively. A minority of non-assortative communities formed a rich club of interneurons bridging sensory/ascending inputs to descending outputs, and those interneurons mediated communication across modules and hierarchical scales.
ocar.future_work: Whether the same hierarchical block structure appears in adult fly or other nano-scale connectomes would test if the larva’s mixed assortative/rich-club architecture is a general developmental solution.

summaries.beginner: This paper groups larval fruit-fly neurons into nested communities using only the wiring, then checks those groups against known cell types. Most groups stay among similar cells, but a small hub club of in-between cells helps messages travel across the brain.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), this study applies a hierarchical weighted stochastic blockmodel to the larval Drosophila connectome. Detected communities partition neurons by function and cell type and mostly interact assortatively, consistent with functional segregation. A small set of communities interact non-assortatively; their neurons form a rich club composed mostly of interneurons that receive sensory/ascending input and send descending output. Polysynaptic signaling is described as following specific trajectories across the hierarchy, with interneurons mediating routes between modules and scales.
summaries.advanced: Community labels are model-based; alternative blockmodels could shift boundaries. Assortativity is the majority pattern, so the rich-club interneuron story concerns a minority of blocks and should not be over-generalized to the whole larva. The abstract does not report how much annotation variance the blocks explain. Communication “trajectories” are inferred from topology, not measured activity.

plain_language_summary: This paper groups larval fruit-fly neurons into nested communities using only the wiring, then checks those groups against known cell types. Most groups stay among similar cells, but a small hub club of in-between cells helps messages travel across the brain.

ocar.opportunity: The first whole-brain connectome of an adult fly, with over 130,000 neurons and millions of synapses, makes brain-wide network statistics tractable rather than regional.
ocar.challenge: Interpreting two- and three-node motifs, rich clubs, and neuropil subnetworks requires combining wiring with neurotransmitter and cell-type annotations and comparing to other animals.
ocar.action: Lin and colleagues computed motif prevalence and strength in the FlyWire whole-brain network, related metrics to neurotransmitter composition and cell types, analyzed rich-club organization, and examined 78 neuropil subnetworks, sharing products in FlyWire Codex.
ocar.resolution: The fly brain is highly recurrent and shows rich-club organization, with about 30% of neurons highly connected; subsets of rich-club neurons are proposed as integrators or broadcasters. The statistics are intended as a foundation for models linking activity to anatomy.
ocar.future_work: Using these motif and rich-club maps to constrain activity models, and testing whether integrator/broadcaster subsets match physiological roles, is the stated next use of the resource.

summaries.beginner: With a whole fruit-fly brain wiring diagram in hand, this paper counts common connection patterns and finds a large club of well-connected cells. About three in ten neurons sit in that highly connected group.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2024), this study computes network statistics on the whole-brain Drosophila connectome of over 130,000 neurons and millions of synapses. The authors quantify two- and three-node motifs and their strengths, relate them to neurotransmitter and cell-type annotations, and compare metrics with wiring diagrams of other animals. They report rich-club organization involving about 30% of the connectome and identify candidate integrator and broadcaster subsets. Subnetwork analyses cover 78 anatomically defined neuropils, with data products in FlyWire Codex.
summaries.advanced: A rich club containing 30% of neurons is unusually large compared with many other networks; interpretation should note that membership depends on degree thresholds not specified in the abstract. Motif comparisons to other animals are mentioned but not enumerated here. Recurrence is a global summary and may differ sharply by neuropil among the 78 regions. Statistics inherit FlyWire proofreading and neurotransmitter-prediction error.

plain_language_summary: With a whole fruit-fly brain wiring diagram in hand, this paper counts common connection patterns and finds a large club of well-connected cells. About three in ten neurons sit in that highly connected group.

ocar.opportunity: Local EM reconstructions inform regional circuits but are inadequate for brain-wide function; a whole adult brain wiring diagram with interoperable annotations was missing.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing chemical synapses among more than a hundred thousand neurons, then annotating classes, types, nerves, hemilineages, and predicted transmitters, is a community-scale proofreading and software problem.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald and the FlyWire consortium present a neuronal wiring diagram of an adult female Drosophila with 5×10⁷ chemical synapses among 139,255 neurons, plus annotations and data products for download, programmatic access, and interactive browsing.
ocar.resolution: They derive a projectome of inter-region projections, trace information flow from sensory and ascending inputs to motor, endocrine, and descending outputs, and illustrate structure-to-behavior analysis by tracing from a subset of photoreceptors to descending motor pathways.
ocar.future_work: The open ecosystem is explicitly framed as setting the stage for large-scale connectome projects in other species.

summaries.beginner: This paper releases a wiring diagram of an entire adult fruit-fly brain: which cells connect, what kinds they are, and roughly what chemical they use. The map is public so others can follow paths from the eyes to the cells that drive movement.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2024), FlyWire presents a whole-brain wiring diagram of an adult female Drosophila melanogaster containing 5×10⁷ chemical synapses between 139,255 neurons, with annotations of cell classes and types, nerves, hemilineages, and predicted neurotransmitters. Data products are interoperable with other fly resources. The authors derive a projectome, analyze information flow from inputs to outputs across hemispheres and between central brain and optic lobes, and trace from a subset of photoreceptors to descending motor pathways as a circuit example. Technologies and the open ecosystem are offered as a template for other species.
summaries.advanced: Neuron and synapse counts are reconstruction products of one female brain and will shift slightly with further proofreading. Neurotransmitter identities are predictions, not direct measurements, as indicated in the abstract. Pathway tracing from a photoreceptor subset is illustrative, not a complete sensorimotor census. Companion papers in the same issue (annotation, network statistics, effectome) should be read alongside this resource paper.

plain_language_summary: This paper releases a wiring diagram of an entire adult fruit-fly brain: which cells connect, what kinds they are, and roughly what chemical they use. The map is public so others can follow paths from the eyes to the cells that drive movement.

ocar.opportunity: A long-standing goal is to read circuit function from form; a vertebrate brainstem wiring diagram plus physiology in the same system makes that test concrete.
ocar.challenge: Dense synaptic reconstructions must be turned into modules and dynamics that can be compared with cellular-resolution activity, not just described anatomically.
ocar.action: Vishwanathan and colleagues reconstructed a synaptic wiring diagram of the larval zebrafish brainstem, identified strongly connected modules, and built a neural-network model directly from that diagram to predict eye-position coding and dynamics, then compared predictions with calcium imaging.
ocar.resolution: Modules were specialized for eye versus body movements. The eye-movement module contained two three-block cycles consistent with positive-feedback attractor dynamics hypothesized for oculomotor control. Model predictions for cellular-resolution coding of eye position and neural dynamics were statistically verified in the imaging data.
ocar.future_work: Applying the same connectome-to-model-to-physiology loop to other vertebrate motor modules would test whether cycle motifs generalize beyond this oculomotor example.

summaries.beginner: Researchers mapped connections in a young zebrafish’s brainstem, then asked whether the wiring could predict how cells encode eye position. The predictions matched calcium-imaging measurements.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Neuroscience (2024), this study reconstructs a synaptic wiring diagram of the larval zebrafish brainstem and uses it to predict function. Strongly connected modules turned out to be specialized for eye versus body movements, and the eye-movement module contained two three-block cycles that can support the positive feedback long hypothesized for low-dimensional oculomotor attractors. A network model built directly from the wiring diagram predicted cellular-resolution eye-position coding and neural dynamics, and those predictions were statistically verified with calcium imaging. The work is presented as a demonstration of connectome-based brain modeling.
summaries.advanced: Verification is statistical agreement with calcium imaging, not a full dynamical-system identification. The model is based on the reconstructed wiring diagram; abstract does not specify which biophysical details were fitted versus frozen. Module specialization for eye versus body is a connectivity finding later aligned with behaviorally associated function. The volume is brainstem, not whole brain, so conclusions are circuit-specific.

plain_language_summary: Researchers mapped connections in a young zebrafish’s brainstem, then asked whether the wiring could predict how cells encode eye position. The predictions matched calcium-imaging measurements.

ocar.opportunity: The whole-brain fly connectome specifies synaptic paths but not how strongly neurons affect one another in vivo—the causal “effectome.”
ocar.challenge: Estimating a causal dynamical model of an entire brain is data-hungry if every possible influence must be measured, and optogenetic experiments cannot exhaustively stimulate every neuron.
ocar.action: Pospisil and colleagues propose an estimator for a linear dynamical model that uses stochastic optogenetic perturbation data, with the connectome as a prior, validate it in connectome-based linear and more biophysical simulations, and analyze the connectome for circuits that dominate the dynamics.
ocar.resolution: Dominant circuits involve only relatively small neuron populations, making neuron-level imaging, stimulation, and identification feasible. The analysis rediscovers known circuits, generates testable dynamical hypotheses, and supports the view that fly whole-brain dynamics arise from many small, largely independent circuits, implying a causal whole-brain model may be obtainable.
ocar.future_work: The paper motivates a real perturbation campaign; collecting the proposed stochastic optogenetic dataset and fitting the estimator in vivo is the remaining empirical step.

summaries.beginner: A fly brain map shows possible routes, not how strongly one cell actually pushes another. This paper argues you can learn those strengths with clever light-based perturbations, because the brain seems to be made of many small, mostly separate circuits.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2024), this study proposes a path from the fly connectome to a causal linear dynamical model (the “effectome”). An estimator would use stochastic optogenetic perturbations, with connectivity as a prior to improve efficiency, and is validated in linear connectome-based simulations and as a linear approximation to more biophysical simulations. Connectome analysis indicates that dynamics-dominating circuits involve relatively small neuron populations and rediscovers known circuits while generating dynamical hypotheses. The authors conclude that whole-brain dynamics look like a large collection of small, largely independent circuits.
summaries.advanced: In vivo perturbation data are not collected here; validation is in simulation. Independence of small circuits is an inference from connectome structure and simulated dynamics, and could fail if unmodeled neuromodulation couples them. The linear estimator approximates nonlinear biophysical simulations; the quality of that approximation is asserted, not quantified in the abstract. Feasibility of neuron-level identification for dominant circuits is a practical claim about population size, not a completed experiment.

plain_language_summary: A fly brain map shows possible routes, not how strongly one cell actually pushes another. This paper argues you can learn those strengths with clever light-based perturbations, because the brain seems to be made of many small, mostly separate circuits.

ocar.opportunity: The ~140,000-neuron FlyWire whole-brain connectome is most useful if neurons can be named as classes, types, and hemilineages and compared with other brains.
ocar.challenge: Cell types proposed from the partial hemibrain volume could not all be reidentified: nearly all hemibrain neurons matched morphologically in FlyWire, but about one-third of proposed types could not be reliably recovered, so a definition robust to individual variation was needed.
ocar.action: Schlegel and colleagues produced a systematic hierarchical annotation of FlyWire, jointly analyzed FlyWire and hemibrain, and defined a cell type as a group of cells each quantitatively more similar to cells in a different brain than to any other cell in the same brain.
ocar.resolution: Of 8,453 annotated cell types, 3,643 were previously proposed in the hemibrain and 4,581 are new, mostly from regions outside that subvolume. The work yields a consensus cell-type atlas, heuristics for connection reliability across brains, and evidence for mushroom-body homeostasis via adjusted excitatory input with a stable excitation/inhibition ratio.
ocar.future_work: The open-source comparative toolchain is meant to be applied to additional fly brains and, later, other species; more than two brains will be required to turn two-animal stereotypy into population statistics.

summaries.beginner: Scientists named the cell types in a whole fruit-fly brain so it can be compared with another fly’s brain. Many types match, but some do not, so they propose a stricter rule: a real type should look more like its partners in another brain than like other cells in the same brain.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2024), this study presents a systematic hierarchical annotation of the approximately 140,000-neuron FlyWire whole-brain connectome, covering neuronal classes, cell types, and developmental hemilineages. Of 8,453 annotated cell types, 3,643 were previously proposed in the hemibrain connectome and 4,581 are new, mostly from regions outside that subvolume. The authors redefine a cell type as groups of cells that are each more similar to cells in a different brain than to any other cell in the same brain, and they validate this definition by jointly analyzing FlyWire and hemibrain. Further analysis yields heuristics for cross-brain connection reliability, documents stereotypy with occasional variation in neuron count and connectivity, and reports mushroom-body homeostasis through adjustments of excitatory input while maintaining the excitation/inhibition ratio.
summaries.advanced: About one-third of hemibrain-proposed types could not be reliably reidentified, which is both a result and a motivation for the new definition; it is not evidence that those types were simply wrong in every case. Comparative claims rest on two connectomes (FlyWire and hemibrain), so “stereotypy” is still a two-animal statement. Connection-reliability heuristics and E/I homeostasis are reported as interpretations of the joint analysis; the abstract does not give the numeric thresholds in this Nature summary (they appear in the companion preprint). The atlas is a consensus resource, not a molecular ground truth.

plain_language_summary: Scientists named the cell types in a whole fruit-fly brain so it can be compared with another fly’s brain. Many types match, but some do not, so they propose a stricter rule: a real type should look more like its partners in another brain than like other cells in the same brain.

ocar.opportunity: A dense wiring diagram of the Drosophila central brain still leaves most motor neurons unmapped, because they sit in the ventral nerve cord, analogous to a spinal cord.
ocar.challenge: Extending full-circuit mapping to behavior requires a VNC connectome at the same morphological and chemical-synapse standard as the brain volumes.
ocar.action: Takemura and colleagues used large-volume EM reconstruction methods previously applied to central brain to generate a dense connectome of the VNC of a male fly.
ocar.resolution: The paper reports that connectome as an extension of the effort to map complete neural circuits for behavior through to motor output.
ocar.future_work: Linking this male VNC wiring to muscle targets and to female VNC reconstructions would test which motor circuits are shared versus sex-specific.

summaries.beginner: To understand movement, you have to map the nerve cord that talks to the muscles, not only the brain. This team built a detailed connection map of a male fruit fly’s ventral nerve cord.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), this study presents a dense wiring diagram of a large portion of the male Drosophila ventral nerve cord. The authors apply previously established large-volume EM reconstruction methods that recover neuron morphology and chemical synapses. The work extends their earlier central-brain connectome toward complete circuits for behavior, because most motor neurons lie in the VNC rather than the brain. The male VNC connectome is the delivered resource.
summaries.advanced: The abstract is short on counts, completeness, and proofreading metrics; it should be read as a resource announcement rather than a circuit-analysis paper. It is a male VNC, so comparison with the later female FANC reconstruction is necessary before generalizing motor architecture. “Dense” and “large portion” are not quantified here. Methods are described as extensions of prior brain technology, not as a new imaging modality.

plain_language_summary: To understand movement, you have to map the nerve cord that talks to the muscles, not only the brain. This team built a detailed connection map of a male fruit fly’s ventral nerve cord.

ocar.opportunity: The first full adult fly brain connectome is difficult to navigate without systematic names for classes, types, and hemilineages linked to the literature.
ocar.challenge: Comparing FlyWire to the hemibrain showed that while cell-type counts and strong connections were largely stable, weights varied and about one-third of hemibrain types could not yet be reliably identified, so types must be defined to survive inter-individual variation.
ocar.action: Schlegel and colleagues hierarchically annotated the ~130,000-neuron FlyWire connectome, validated 3,094 hemibrain types as consensus, proposed 1,458 new types, and jointly analyzed both connectomes under a cross-brain similarity definition of cell type.
ocar.resolution: They report simple interpretation heuristics (connections stronger than 10 unitary synapses or >1% of a target’s input are highly conserved), striking mushroom-body Kenyon-cell count differences, and evidence for excitatory-input homeostasis with preserved E/I ratio, plus an open-source comparative toolchain.
ocar.future_work: The same consensus definition and toolchain need additional brains to distinguish true type instability from two-sample matching failures.

summaries.beginner: This preprint names the cell types in a whole fly brain and checks them against an earlier partial map. Strong connections tend to match, weaker ones vary, and the authors suggest a type should look more like the same cells in another brain than like other cells in its own brain.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), this companion annotation paper reports systematic hierarchical labeling of the ~130,000-neuron FlyWire connectome, including 4,552 cell types: 3,094 consensus validations of hemibrain types and 1,458 new types, mostly because FlyWire is whole-brain. Comparison found largely stable type counts and strong connections but surprisingly variable weights; connections stronger than 10 unitary synapses or providing >1% of input to a target were highly conserved. About one-third of hemibrain-proposed types could not yet be reliably identified in FlyWire, motivating a definition of types as groups more similar to cells in another brain than to other cells in the same brain. Evidence is also reported for mushroom-body Kenyon-cell number differences and functional homeostasis of excitatory input with a stable excitation/inhibition ratio.
summaries.advanced: This preprint and the 2024 Nature annotation paper are closely related; type counts differ (4,552 vs 8,453) because the journal version expanded the atlas. Heuristics (10 synapses; >1% input) are offered as practical conservation rules, not laws. Kenyon-cell number “almost twice as numerous in FlyWire as the hemibrain” is a large biological or technical discrepancy that the abstract treats as biological individuality plus homeostasis. About one-third unmatched hemibrain types could reflect annotation, volume coverage, or true polymorphism.

plain_language_summary: This preprint names the cell types in a whole fly brain and checks them against an earlier partial map. Strong connections tend to match, weaker ones vary, and the authors suggest a type should look more like the same cells in another brain than like other cells in its own brain.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic connectivity determines how each cortical cell type participates in the circuit, but rules at distinct-type resolution have been difficult to map.
ocar.challenge: Doing so requires dense millimeter-scale EM, classification of inhibitory targeting, and a data-driven excitatory taxonomy from morphology and synaptic input.
