ocar.action: Schneider-Mizell and colleagues mapped all inhibitory neurons among 1,352 densely segmented cells across all layers of mouse visual cortex, reconstructing more than 70,000 inhibitory synapses, using volumetric EM.
ocar.resolution: Connectivity revealed a disinhibitory specialist targeting basket cells, widespread interneuron specificity for intermingled excitatory subpopulations, and motif groups that collectively innervate perisomatic and dendritic compartments of the same excitatory targets.
ocar.future_work: Aligning these EM-defined types with multimodal atlases is presented as the next use of the census.

summaries.beginner: This preprint maps how inhibitory cells connect inside a column of mouse visual cortex. It finds that inhibition is organized into repeating targeting patterns, not a uniform blanket.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), this study uses millimeter-scale volumetric EM to reconstruct inhibitory connectivity among 1,352 densely segmented neurons spanning all layers of mouse visual cortex, with more than 70,000 synapses. Inhibitory neurons are classified by relative targeting of dendritic compartments and other inhibitory cells; excitatory neurons are classified from morphology and synaptic-input properties. Results include a disinhibitory specialist that targets basket cells, widespread targeting specificity, and motif groups jointly covering soma and dendrites of the same excitatory cells. The census is offered as a foundation for linking multimodal atlases to cortical wiring.
summaries.advanced: This is the preprint counterpart of the 2025 Nature inhibitory-census paper, with the same 1,352-cell and >70,000-synapse figures. Findings should not be double-counted as independent replications. Classification is structural and data-driven, not molecular. Specificity among spatially intermingled targets is a key claim; the abstract does not give a single selectivity statistic.

plain_language_summary: This preprint maps how inhibitory cells connect inside a column of mouse visual cortex. It finds that inhibition is organized into repeating targeting patterns, not a uniform blanket.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes now give complete wiring of some circuits, but dynamical parameters of each neuron and synapse remain unknown, raising the question of how far connectivity alone can go.
ocar.challenge: A model of 64 fly optic-lobe motion-pathway cell types can be wired from measurements yet still has unknown single-neuron and single-synapse parameters that must be set somehow.
ocar.action: Lappalainen and colleagues built a mechanistic network with experimentally determined connectivity, then optimized the unknown parameters with deep-learning methods so the network could detect visual motion, and compared predicted activity with published measurements.
ocar.resolution: Model predictions agreed with experimental neural activity across 24 studies. The authors argue the strategy is more likely to succeed when neurons are sparsely connected, a widely observed feature of biological networks.
ocar.future_work: The paper’s own testable predictions for each neuron invite new recordings; success outside the motion pathway would test whether sparsity-plus-connectivity is generally sufficient.

summaries.beginner: Even with a complete wiring diagram, we usually do not know how strong each connection is. This team fills in those unknowns so a fly vision circuit can detect motion, then checks the model’s cell-by-cell guesses against many past experiments.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), this study constructs a deep mechanistic network of 64 cell types in the Drosophila optic-lobe motion pathways using experimentally determined connectivity, leaving single-neuron and single-synapse parameters unknown. Those parameters are optimized with deep-learning techniques so the network detects visual motion. The resulting model makes detailed predictions for each neuron, and those predictions agreed with experimental measurements across 24 studies. The authors suggest the approach works because biological networks are sparsely connected.
summaries.advanced: Agreement with 24 studies is a strong consistency claim but is not a prospectively registered test on held-out cell types. Parameter optimization for a motion-detection task can overfit task performance while still matching published response signs. Connectivity is “experimentally determined” for the 64 types included; omitted cells and unmeasured synapses remain degrees of freedom. The sparsity argument is comparative/theoretical in the abstract, not a controlled ablation of dense versus sparse graphs in vivo.

plain_language_summary: Even with a complete wiring diagram, we usually do not know how strong each connection is. This team fills in those unknowns so a fly vision circuit can detect motion, then checks the model’s cell-by-cell guesses against many past experiments.

ocar.opportunity: Human cortical grey matter can be about 3 mm thick, so synapse-level circuit analysis of patient tissue needs reliable preservation of volumes larger than the typical 1 mm³ connectomic block.
ocar.challenge: Larger human samples are limited by access to fresh biopsies, ultrastructure including extracellular space, and uniform heavy-metal staining throughout the block.
ocar.action: Karlupia and colleagues describe an immersion fixation, heavy-metal staining, and tissue-processing method developed on neurosurgical samples obtained during deep-brain-stimulation lead placement, and they apply it to human and rodent surgical brain tissue.
ocar.resolution: The method consistently provided excellent ultrastructure in 2 × 2 × 2 mm³ samples and in volumes up to 37 mm³ with one dimension ≤ 2 mm, enabling synapse-level analysis in psychiatric and neurologic patient samples.
ocar.future_work: Using these larger, uniformly stained biopsies to reconstruct disease-associated circuits, not only to demonstrate ultrastructure, is the intended clinical next step.

summaries.beginner: Human cortex is thicker than the small cubes usually used for connection mapping, and the tissue is hard to preserve. This paper describes a staining method that keeps fine structure intact in larger surgical samples from patients.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Biological Psychiatry (2023), this study presents an immersion-fixation and heavy-metal staining protocol for EM connectomics of human brain biopsies. Samples come from neurosurgical patients during deep-brain-stimulation lead placement. The method is reported to give excellent ultrastructure, including extracellular space, throughout human and rodent surgical samples of 2 × 2 × 2 mm³ and volumes up to 37 mm³ provided one dimension is ≤ 2 mm. The authors argue this should allow synapse-level circuit analysis in psychiatric and neurologic disorders.
summaries.advanced: “Excellent ultrastructure” is a qualitative claim; the abstract does not report synapse-detection accuracy or reconstruction completeness. The 37 mm³ success condition (one dimension ≤ 2 mm) means the method is still slab-limited rather than an arbitrary 3 mm-thick cube. Tissue is surgical, so disease and medication effects remain confounds for “circuit analysis in patients.” Rodent results are mentioned as parallel validation, not a full comparative study.

plain_language_summary: Human cortex is thicker than the small cubes usually used for connection mapping, and the tissue is hard to preserve. This paper describes a staining method that keeps fine structure intact in larger surgical samples from patients.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain EM connectomes now provide high-resolution morphology and connectivity, creating a cheaper path to neuron classification than anatomical, physiological, or molecular assays alone.
ocar.challenge: Few models jointly use skeleton morphology and circuit topology, and public classification datasets from volume EM have been scarce.
ocar.action: Liao, Wan, and Du propose NeuNet, combining a skeleton encoder (1D convolution on skeleton points), a connectome encoder (graph neural network on circuit topology), and a readout that fuses both, and they release two reprocessed VEM classification datasets from human cortex and Drosophila brain.
ocar.resolution: The model achieved accuracies of 0.9169 and 0.9363 on the human-cortex and Drosophila datasets respectively.
ocar.future_work: Testing whether the same dual encoder generalizes to other EM labs and finer type inventories would show if connectivity adds reliable type signal beyond morphology.

summaries.beginner: Telling neuron types apart is slow if you need extra lab assays for every cell. This computer method looks at each cell’s shape and who it connects to, and it classifies cells in human cortex and fly brain datasets with high accuracy.
summaries.intermediate: Published at AAAI (2023), this study presents NeuNet, a neuron-classification framework that jointly encodes neuronal skeletons and brain-circuit topology with permutation-invariant encoders. A skeleton encoder uses one-dimensional convolution on skeleton point data; a connectome encoder uses a graph neural network; a readout fuses the two. The authors reprocess and release two volume-EM datasets from human brain cortex and Drosophila brain, reporting classification accuracies of 0.9169 and 0.9363. Code and data are public.
summaries.advanced: Accuracies are dataset-specific and the abstract does not specify the number of classes or class balance, so they are not comparable to cell-typing in FlyWire-scale atlases without reading the paper. Permutation invariance addresses neuron labeling but not EM segmentation error in the skeletons themselves. Dual-encoder gains versus morphology-only or connectivity-only ablations are not quantified in the abstract. Human and fly datasets are newly released here; independent splits and label ontologies will determine reuse.

plain_language_summary: Telling neuron types apart is slow if you need extra lab assays for every cell. This computer method looks at each cell’s shape and who it connects to, and it classifies cells in human cortex and fly brain datasets with high accuracy.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic reconstructions still depend on expert labeling, and many labs need deep-learning segmentation without writing code or buying specialized clusters.
ocar.challenge: State-of-the-art automatic segmentation is powerful but poorly wrapped for MATLAB users who already proofread in tools such as VAST on ordinary desktops.
ocar.action: Pavarino and colleagues built mEMbrain, a MATLAB GUI API to VAST that covers ground-truth generation, preprocessing, deep-network training, and on-the-fly predictions for proofreading, and they release ~180 hours of expert annotations (>1.2 GB) across five datasets from four animals plus four pretrained networks.
ocar.resolution: The tool is reported to work across species, scales, nervous-system regions, and developmental stages on Linux and Windows commodity desktops, aiming at affordable, no-coding lab-based reconstructions.
ocar.future_work: Whether mEMbrain’s desktop workflow remains competitive as transformer and foundation-model segmenters mature will determine its long-term role versus cloud pipelines.

summaries.beginner: Tracing cells in electron-microscope volumes usually takes coding skill and big computers. mEMbrain is a point-and-click MATLAB helper that trains a recognizer on your labels and runs on an ordinary lab computer.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2023), this study presents mEMbrain, an interactive MATLAB tool for connectomic segmentation that wraps labeling, preprocessing, deep-network training, and on-the-fly prediction as an API to VAST. It runs on Linux and Windows commodity desktops and was tested on datasets spanning species, scales, regions, and developmental stages. The authors release about 180 hours of expert annotations from four animals and five datasets (>1.2 GB of annotated EM images) plus four pretrained networks. The goal is lab-based instance segmentation without user coding.
summaries.advanced: This is a usability and resource paper; the abstract does not report leaderboard scores against current 3D CNNs. Integration with VAST is a strength for existing Lichtman-lab workflows and a limitation for labs on other proofreading stacks. Annotation hours (~180) measure effort, not label quality. “Affordable connectomics” here means software accessibility, not reduced EM acquisition cost.

plain_language_summary: Tracing cells in electron-microscope volumes usually takes coding skill and big computers. mEMbrain is a point-and-click MATLAB helper that trains a recognizer on your labels and runs on an ordinary lab computer.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM can map circuits but lacks molecular labels that identify cell types and functional proteins; volumetric CLEM could add those layers if labeling worked in thick, EM-compatible tissue.
ocar.challenge: Standard immunohistochemistry uses detergents that ruin ultrastructure, and multiplexed fluorescence in the same EM volume is difficult.
ocar.action: Han and colleagues developed detergent-free multiplexed labeling with small fluorescent scFv probes, generated eight scFvs against common neuronal markers, and imaged six probes in cerebellar Crus 1 by confocal spectral unmixing followed by ssEM.
ocar.resolution: The correlated volume retained excellent ultrastructure with superimposed fluorescence, documenting a poorly described cerebellar cell type, two mossy-fiber terminal types, and the subcellular localization of one ion channel. Because scFvs can be derived from existing monoclonal antibodies, the approach is presented as scalable to many molecular overlays.
ocar.future_work: Expanding the scFv panel and applying multiplexed vCLEM outside cerebellum would test whether the cytology gains generalize to other circuits.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope maps show shape and connections but not which proteins a cell contains. This team uses tiny antibody pieces that glow, so they can see several proteins and the fine structure in the same piece of mouse cerebellum.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on Research Square (2023), this study presents multiplexed volumetric CLEM using fluorescent single-chain variable fragments without detergent permeabilization. Eight scFvs were generated against GFP, GFAP, calbindin, parvalbumin, Kv1.2, vGluT1, PSD-95, and neuropeptide Y. Six probes were imaged in mouse cerebellar Crus 1 with confocal spectral unmixing, then the same sample was imaged by serial-section EM, yielding aligned molecular and ultrastructural maps. Applications include documenting a poorly described cerebellar cell type, two mossy-fiber terminal types, and subcellular ion-channel localization.
summaries.advanced: “Excellent ultrastructure” is qualitative; penetration depth and labeling completeness versus conventional IHC are not quantified in the abstract. Six-plex in one volume is the demonstration; eight scFvs were generated. Scalability to “hundreds” of probes is a prospect from monoclonal conversion, not a result shown here. Findings are from cerebellar cortex; cortical applicability is not demonstrated in this abstract.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope maps show shape and connections but not which proteins a cell contains. This team uses tiny antibody pieces that glow, so they can see several proteins and the fine structure in the same piece of mouse cerebellum.

ocar.opportunity: Cubic-millimeter EM volumes contain enormous numbers of synapses whose structural diversity is too large to annotate by hand.
ocar.challenge: Supervised synapse classifiers need labels, but most synapses in a millimeter-scale volume will never be manually marked.
ocar.action: Wilson and Babadi introduce SynapseCLR, a self-supervised contrastive method on 3D EM, trained on mouse visual-cortex synapses, and use the embeddings for one-shot detection of defective segmentations, similarity search, and imputation of annotations.
ocar.resolution: Representations separated synapses by appearance and functionally important structural annotations. With manual annotation of only 0.2% of synapses, excitatory versus inhibitory type could be assigned with >99.8% accuracy to individual synapses and highly truncated neurites. Unsupervised analysis of the representation manifold revealed intrinsic variation axes including inhibitory subtype information.
ocar.future_work: Applying the same contrastive embeddings to other cortical areas and EM pipelines would test whether the 0.2%-label imputation trick is dataset-specific.

summaries.beginner: There are far too many synapses in a cubic millimeter of brain to label by hand. This method learns synapse appearance from unlabeled images, then uses a tiny number of labels to tell excitatory from inhibitory contacts with very high accuracy.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Patterns (2023), this study presents SynapseCLR, a self-supervised contrastive learning method for 3D EM synapses in mouse primary visual cortex (MICrONS). Embeddings separate synapses by appearance and by structural annotations, and they support one-shot identification of defective segmentations, dataset-wide similarity queries, and imputation of labels from manual annotation of only 0.2% of synapses. Excitatory versus inhibitory neuronal types could be assigned with >99.8% accuracy to individual synapses and highly truncated neurites. Unsupervised exploration of the representation manifold recovered intrinsic axes of variation, including inhibitory subtype information.
summaries.advanced: The >99.8% E/I figure is striking and is tied to this dataset and annotation protocol; the abstract does not report confidence intervals or an external test volume. Truncated-neurite typing is a practical gain for incomplete reconstructions. Inhibitory subtype signal in the unsupervised manifold is reported as present, not as a full subtype classifier with accuracies. Contrastive learning on already-detected synapses assumes a synapse detector; errors there propagate.

plain_language_summary: There are far too many synapses in a cubic millimeter of brain to label by hand. This method learns synapse appearance from unlabeled images, then uses a tiny number of labels to tell excitatory from inhibitory contacts with very high accuracy.

ocar.opportunity: Inferring simple design principles of connectomes would link development, architecture, and function across species, but most generative models use many assumed biological features.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear how few measurable features suffice to predict synapses, degrees, motifs, and—critically—circuit computation.
ocar.action: Haber and colleagues learned probabilistic generative models of the zebrafish olfactory bulb, part of mouse visual cortex, and C. elegans, then simulated synthetic zebrafish olfactory circuits and compared their odor computation to the real circuit, adding latent features where models failed.
ocar.resolution: Models using a surprisingly small number of simple biological and physical features accurately predicted individual synapses and strengths, in/out-degree distributions, and motif frequencies. Synthetic zebrafish olfactory circuits replicated the real circuit’s odor-response computation. Systematic model failures, patched with latent features, revealed missing design ingredients.
ocar.future_work: Exporting the same small-feature generative tests to additional complete connectomes would show whether “a small number of design principles” is a general result or specific to these three circuits.

summaries.beginner: This paper asks whether a few simple rules can rebuild the wiring of a fish smell circuit, a piece of mouse visual cortex, and the worm nervous system. The simple models copy many wiring statistics, and a fake fish circuit even copies how the real one responds to odors.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), this study learns probabilistic generative models for connectomes of the zebrafish olfactory bulb, part of mouse visual cortex, and C. elegans. A small number of biological and physical features predicted synapse existence and strength, degree distributions, and subnetwork motif frequencies. Simulated zebrafish olfactory circuits replicated the computation performed by the real circuit in response to olfactory cues. Failures of the models were used diagnostically by adding latent features to uncover missing design principles.
summaries.advanced: “Surprisingly small number” is not enumerated in the abstract. Functional replication is reported for zebrafish olfactory computation, not for mouse cortex or C. elegans behavior. Mouse visual cortex is only “part of” the area, so it is not a whole-circuit generative test. Latent features that rescue failures are informative but also show the small observed feature set is incomplete.

plain_language_summary: This paper asks whether a few simple rules can rebuild the wiring of a fish smell circuit, a piece of mouse visual cortex, and the worm nervous system. The simple models copy many wiring statistics, and a fake fish circuit even copies how the real one responds to odors.

ocar.opportunity: X-ray holographic nanotomography can image myelinated long-range axons over larger fields of view than EM, offering a path to brain-wide projectomes the authors call XPRESS.
ocar.challenge: XNH volumes are typically lower resolution and larger FOV than EM, so accurate axon segmentation is unsolved, and voxel-wise ground truth is slow to paint while skeletons are faster and already suffice for connectivity.
ocar.action: Nguyen and colleagues pose a public challenge with volumetric XNH of mouse cortical white-matter axons, a small voxel-wise labeled volume, a larger skeleton-annotated volume, and an evaluation metric based on agreement with ground-truth skeletons.
ocar.resolution: The resource is designed to spur methods that learn from skeletons rather than dense voxel labels, which would remove a key bottleneck for XNH projectomics.
ocar.future_work: Winning skeleton-trained segmenters still need to be shown on tracts beyond the released cortical white-matter volumes before XNH can map a whole-mouse projectome.

summaries.beginner: X-rays can scan long-distance brain cables over bigger regions than electron microscopes, but computers still struggle to trace those cables. This challenge gives X-ray volumes and simpler “stick figure” traces so teams can train better tracers.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on arXiv (2023), this paper introduces the XPRESS challenge for segmenting axons in X-ray holographic nanotomography of mouse cortical white matter. The authors argue XNH is suited to myelinated projection tracts that EM cannot currently cover brain-wide. They release volumetric images with a small voxel-wise ground-truth region and a larger skeleton-annotated region, and they evaluate submissions on agreement with skeletons. The design encourages methods that train on skeletons rather than exhaustive voxel labels.
summaries.advanced: This is a challenge announcement, not a completed segmentation method. Evaluation on skeletons can score topology while missing caliber and myelin errors. The abstract does not report baseline scores. XNH projectomics is motivated as complementary to EM connectomics; it will not replace synaptic-resolution local circuits.

plain_language_summary: X-rays can scan long-distance brain cables over bigger regions than electron microscopes, but computers still struggle to trace those cables. This challenge gives X-ray volumes and simpler “stick figure” traces so teams can train better tracers.

ocar.opportunity: Petascale reconstructions finally let neuroscientists search for small repeating connectivity motifs, but finding and visually relating those subgraphs to 3D neurons is still painful.
ocar.challenge: Motifs may involve only 2–6 neurons, yet they sit in huge graphs, and experts must jump between abstract topology and detailed meshes and synapses.
ocar.action: Troidl and colleagues built Vimo, an interactive tool to sketch motifs with structural constraints, query large connectomes, render motif instances, morph continuously from anatomy to motif abstraction, and search motif chains.
ocar.resolution: In a user study and a case study with seven experts on a fruit-fly connectome of more than 21,000 neurons and 20 million synapses, Vimo enabled hypothesis generation and confirmation through fast iteration and connectivity highlighting.
ocar.future_work: Scaling interactive motif search from this 21,000-neuron fly volume to whole adult brains with >100,000 neurons will stress both query engines and the focus-and-context rendering.

summaries.beginner: Scientists often look for small repeating wiring patterns in giant brain maps. Vimo lets them draw a pattern, find matches, and see those cells in 3D, sliding from realistic shapes to a simple circuit sketch.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), this study presents Vimo, a visual analysis system for neuronal connectivity motifs and motif chains in large brain networks. Users sketch motifs, add structural constraints on neurons and synapses, query connectomes, and inspect instances in high-resolution 3D with a continuous focus-and-context abstraction. Motif chains—repeated use of a motif two to four times—are also supported. Evaluation with seven domain experts on a Drosophila connectome of more than 21,000 neurons and 20 million synapses found that the tool sped hypothesis generation and confirmation.
summaries.advanced: The evaluation is a user/case study, not a benchmark of motif-mining completeness. The fly volume cited (>21,000 neurons) is smaller than whole-adult FlyWire; interactive performance on larger graphs is unstated. Motif sketches encode expert hypotheses, so the tool finds instances of asked patterns rather than discovering unexpected motifs unsupervised. Rendering abstractions could hide ultrastructural cues experts sometimes need.

plain_language_summary: Scientists often look for small repeating wiring patterns in giant brain maps. Vimo lets them draw a pattern, find matches, and see those cells in 3D, sliding from realistic shapes to a simple circuit sketch.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans now has both a synapse-resolution connectome and nervous-system-wide activity maps, making a systematic structure–function comparison possible.
ocar.challenge: Which graph features—local motifs, triplet structure, hubs, shared inputs, or weights—actually predict correlated activity on a global scale remains unclear.
ocar.action: Uzel, Kato, and Zimmer compared graph features in the C. elegans connectome with correlations in brain-wide neuronal dynamics and inhibited hub neurons to test their role in global correlations.
ocar.resolution: Few local connectivity motifs, and mostly non-local features such as triplet motifs and input similarity, predicted functional relationships; connection strength and amount of common input did not improve those predictions, suggesting topology suffices. Hub neurons were central to the relevant features, and inhibiting multiple hubs specifically disrupted brain-wide correlations.
ocar.future_work: Identifying which hub set is necessary versus redundant, and whether the same non-local predictors hold under more stimulus conditions, would refine the proposed anatomical substrate for global dynamics.

summaries.beginner: In the worm, knowing two cells share a connection does not fully predict whether they fire together. This study finds that broader wiring patterns and a few hub cells matter more, and silencing several hubs breaks whole-brain coordination.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Current Biology (2022), this study systematically compares C. elegans connectome graph features with nervous-system-wide activity correlations. Local motifs were weak predictors relative to non-local features such as triplet motifs and input similarity. Connection strength and the amount of common input did not improve predictions, pointing to topology rather than weights. Hub neurons were key to those graph features, and inhibiting multiple hubs specifically disrupted brain-wide correlations.
summaries.advanced: The organism field is empty in the catalog row, but the abstract is unambiguously C. elegans. Functional relationships are operationalized as activity correlations, which mix shared drive with true coupling. Hub inhibition that disrupts global correlations is causal support, yet the abstract does not say how many hubs or which identities. Weight not helping could reflect coarse synapse counts as well as true topological dominance.

plain_language_summary: In the worm, knowing two cells share a connection does not fully predict whether they fire together. This study finds that broader wiring patterns and a few hub cells matter more, and silencing several hubs breaks whole-brain coordination.

ocar.opportunity: High-resolution connectomics now spans a pipeline from acquisition through circuit analysis, and each stage produces large, complex data that visualization can make usable.
ocar.challenge: Methods are scattered across acquisition, automated segmentation, proofreading, exploration, and analysis, and newcomers need a map of tools, open datasets, and remaining gaps.
ocar.action: Beyer and colleagues survey visualization methods integrated at each pipeline step, review open-science initiatives and public datasets, and discuss open challenges.
ocar.resolution: The state-of-the-art report organizes how visualization is currently used from data acquisition to circuit analysis and outlines possible future directions for the field.
ocar.future_work: The authors highlight remaining visualization challenges as volumes and reconstructions continue to grow; addressing those gaps is the agenda they set rather than a single follow-up experiment.

summaries.beginner: Making sense of huge neuron maps requires good pictures and interactive tools at every step, from imaging to proofreading to circuit diagrams. This survey reviews those tools and what is still hard.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Computer Graphics Forum (2022), this state-of-the-art report surveys visualization and analysis methods for high-resolution connectomics. The authors define pipeline steps from data acquisition through automated segmentation, proofreading, interactive exploration, and circuit analysis, and they review how visualization is integrated at each step. They also survey open-science initiatives, open-source tools, and public datasets. The paper closes with open challenges and possible future directions.
summaries.advanced: As a survey, it does not present a new algorithm or quantitative user study in the abstract. Coverage quality depends on the literature snapshot of 2022 and will omit later FlyWire/CAVE-scale web tools. “High-resolution connectomics” here means EM-scale work rather than MRI connectomics. Recommendations are field-level, not a single prioritized roadmap with resources.

plain_language_summary: Making sense of huge neuron maps requires good pictures and interactive tools at every step, from imaging to proofreading to circuit diagrams. This survey reviews those tools and what is still hard.

ocar.opportunity: Large-scale EM reconstructions are advancing quickly, but synapse detection in cerebellum has lagged behind neuronal reconstruction.
ocar.challenge: Cerebellar molecular-layer synapses must be found on reconstructed fragments whose types can be identified, and pre/post sides plus excitatory/inhibitory class must be assigned automatically.
ocar.action: Park and colleagues extract contacts between reconstructed fragments and classify them as synaptic or not using type information and two deep-learning models, then assign polarity and E/I type.
ocar.resolution: On a mouse cerebellar molecular-layer test volume containing 508 synapses, accuracy was estimated at 0.955 F1. The method was used to measure synapse size and number and to inspect subcellular connectivity among CML fragments.
ocar.future_work: The authors note that exploiting tissue-specific properties can extend to other brain regions, which is the natural generalization test.

summaries.beginner: Finding synapses automatically is still harder than tracing cells, especially in cerebellum. This method uses cell-type hints and two neural networks to mark synapses in mouse cerebellar tissue with high agreement to a test set.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2022), this study presents an automated synapse detector for the mouse cerebellar molecular layer. Contacts between reconstructed neuronal fragments are classified as synaptic or not with type information and two deep-learning models, and each synapse is assigned pre- and postsynaptic sides plus excitatory or inhibitory type. Accuracy on a test volume containing 508 synapses was estimated at 0.955 F1. The authors demonstrate usability by measuring synapse size and number and inspecting subcellular connectivity.
summaries.advanced: F1 = 0.955 is for one CML test volume of 508 synapses; performance elsewhere is not reported. The method assumes reconstructed fragments with identifiable types, so it is not a from-pixels synapse detector on raw EM alone. Tissue-specific design is both the source of accuracy and the barrier to immediate transfer. E/I assignment quality is not separately scored in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Finding synapses automatically is still harder than tracing cells, especially in cerebellum. This method uses cell-type hints and two neural networks to mark synapses in mouse cerebellar tissue with high agreement to a test set.

ocar.opportunity: A whole larval zebrafish brain at synaptic resolution, with automated neuron and synapse reconstructions, would found circuit analysis in a vertebrate with rich visual behavior.
ocar.challenge: Dense reconstruction needs high-resolution EM of an entire brain plus tools to trace neurites and validate automated synapses against TEM and light-microscopic reconstructions.
ocar.action: Svara and colleagues sectioned and imaged a larval zebrafish brain by SBF-SEM at 14 × 14 × 25 nm³, segmented it with flood-filling networks, automated chemical-synapse detection, stored neurons in a queryable address book, and reconstructed identified visual circuits in a specimen that had also been imaged with two-photon calcium imaging.
ocar.resolution: They reconstructed a network of 208 neurons involved in visual motion processing, mostly in pretectum, and mapped all 407 pre- and postsynaptic partners of two superficial tectal interneurons. The resource is presented as a foundation for synaptic-resolution circuit analyses in zebrafish.
ocar.future_work: Expanding automated reconstruction from the demonstrated circuits to more of the larval brain, and relating the 208-cell motion network to the same animal’s physiology, are the immediate uses of the volume.

summaries.beginner: Researchers sliced and imaged a whole baby zebrafish brain in an electron microscope, then let computers outline cells and synapses. They used the map to reconstruct a motion-vision network and all partners of two tectal cells.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Methods (2022), this resource paper presents a serial block-face EM dataset of the whole larval zebrafish brain at 14 × 14 × 25 nm³, segmented with flood-filling networks and automatic chemical-synapse detection. Results were validated against transmission EM and light-microscopic reconstructions. Neurons and connections are stored in a queryable digital address book. The authors reconstructed 208 neurons involved in visual motion processing, most in pretectum and previously characterized by two-photon imaging in the same specimen, and mapped all 407 synaptic partners of two superficial tectal interneurons.
summaries.advanced: “Whole larval zebrafish brain” is the imaged volume; dense proofread completeness is not claimed for every neuron. The 208- and 407-neuron analyses are targeted circuits, not a whole-brain connectome release in the fly sense. Same-specimen two-photon data is a rare alignment opportunity; the abstract does not quantify cross-modal registration error. Voxel size 14 × 14 × 25 nm³ is coarser than some fly EM volumes, which may affect thin-process completeness.

plain_language_summary: Researchers sliced and imaged a whole baby zebrafish brain in an electron microscope, then let computers outline cells and synapses. They used the map to reconstruct a motion-vision network and all partners of two tectal cells.

ocar.opportunity: Mouse cortex is the dominant experimental model, but whether local synaptic circuits match human and macaque cortex has not been tested at connectomic resolution.
ocar.challenge: Human tissue is usually epilepsy-related; comparing species requires 3D EM of nonepileptic surgical access tissue plus macaque and mouse volumes scored with the same cell-type and synapse pipeline.
ocar.action: Loomba and colleagues acquired 3D EM from human temporal/frontal and macaque temporal/parietal cortex (nonepileptic surgical or non-pathological tissue) and compared connectomes with five mouse cortical datasets, analyzing ~1.6 million synapses.
ocar.resolution: A ~2.5-fold increase in interneurons in human versus mouse was not matched by a commensurate rise in inhibitory-versus-excitatory input onto pyramidal cells. Pyramidal total synaptic input rose only modestly (~12,000 in mouse to ~15,000 in human). Instead, bipolar-type interneuron-targeting interneurons expanded, yielding about a 10-fold larger interneuron-to-interneuron network in human cortex.
ocar.future_work: Whether this expanded IN–IN network reflects new interneuron subtypes or scaled existing types, and how it behaves in disease, is left as the next question.

summaries.beginner: Human cortex has many more inhibitory cells than mouse cortex, but the main output cells do not simply receive more inhibition. Instead, a network of inhibitory cells talking to other inhibitory cells is much larger in human samples.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2022), this study compares 3D EM connectomes from mouse, macaque, and human cortex. Human/macaque samples include nonepileptic surgical access tissue and a macaque without known brain pathology. Despite a ~2.5-fold increase in interneurons from mouse to human, inhibitory-to-excitatory synaptic balance onto pyramidal cells was not substantially altered, and total pyramidal synaptic input increased only from about 12,000 to about 15,000. The principal change was an expansion of interneuron-targeting interneurons and their selectivity, producing about a 10-fold larger interneuron-to-interneuron network in human cortex. Analyzed connectomes comprised about 1.6 million synapses.
summaries.advanced: Human n is two individuals (temporal and frontal) plus two macaque regions; this is connectomic screening, not a population study. Surgical access tissue can still differ from true “normal” cortex. The 10-fold IN–IN expansion is the headline evolutionary claim and depends on bipolar-type classification and targeting measurements. Pyramidal input counts (~12k vs ~15k) argue against synapse number simply scaling with cortical thickness; remaining dendrites outside each volume still bound those totals.

plain_language_summary: Human cortex has many more inhibitory cells than mouse cortex, but the main output cells do not simply receive more inhibition. Instead, a network of inhibitory cells talking to other inhibitory cells is much larger in human samples.

ocar.opportunity: Rapidly growing synaptic-resolution EM connectomes, now annotated with gene expression, activity, behavior, and development, can test hypotheses of circuit function in insect behavior.
ocar.challenge: It remains unclear which circuit features are robust across individuals versus variable, and how comparative connectomics across development, experience, sex, and species should be done.
ocar.action: Galili, Jefferis, and Costa review how improved acquisition and matching methods have revealed hierarchical, recurrent, multisensory modules in learned and innate olfaction, navigation, and sexual behavior.
ocar.resolution: Connectomics has already shown interconnected modules with hierarchy, recurrence, and sensory integration in those behaviors. The authors identify individual-to-individual comparison and comparative connectomics across conditions as key research areas for linking connectivity to brain function.
ocar.future_work: The review itself nominates comparative connectomes across development, experience, sex, and species as the work needed to lock those links down.

summaries.beginner: This short review explains how detailed insect brain maps are starting to show why flies smell, navigate, and court as they do. The next big job is comparing maps across individuals and species to see what stays the same.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Current Opinion in Insect Science (2022), this review discusses how synaptic-resolution EM datasets and improved neuronal matching now combine connectivity with gene expression, activity, behavior, and development. In learned and innate olfaction, navigation, and sexual behavior, connectomics has revealed interconnected modules with hierarchical structure, recurrence, and integration of sensory streams. Comparing individual connectomes to separate robust from variable features is highlighted as a key area, as is comparative work across development, experience, sex, and species. The authors argue those comparisons will link neuronal connectivity to brain function.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/review with a short abstract; it does not present new reconstructions. Examples (olfaction, navigation, sexual behavior) are illustrative of a 2022 snapshot. “More complete connectomes” is a field trend, not a quantified completeness metric. Recommendations for comparative connectomics anticipate later FlyWire–hemibrain comparisons but do not perform them here.

plain_language_summary: This short review explains how detailed insect brain maps are starting to show why flies smell, navigate, and court as they do. The next big job is comparing maps across individuals and species to see what stays the same.

ocar.opportunity: The octopus vertical lobe mediates long-term memory, offering a chance to compare a behaviorally advanced molluscan memory circuit with associative networks in other animals.
ocar.challenge: The VL’s cellular inventory, interneuron types, modulatory elements, and synaptic motifs were not mapped at EM connectome resolution.
ocar.action: Bidel and colleagues analyzed a serial-section EM connectome of the Octopus vulgaris vertical lobe, reconstructing input axons and two amacrine types (simple and complex) and their feedforward architecture.
ocar.resolution: About 1.8 million sensory-input axons sparsely innervate two parallel, interconnected feedforward networks. Simple AMs are 89.3% of 25 million AMs, each receiving input from a single input neuron on a non-bifurcating neurite (~12 SAMs per input neuron). Complex AMs (1.6%) integrate multiple inputs and are interpreted as providing balancing inhibition. The VL appears to support associative learning via strictly feedforward flow, sharing some features with other animals while remaining unique.
ocar.future_work: Physiological tests of the proposed SAM “memorization” versus CAM “sharpening” split would confirm whether the feedforward story holds in vivo.

summaries.beginner: Octopuses learn using a brain region called the vertical lobe. This map shows two kinds of tiny cells: many simple ones that each listen to a single incoming fiber, and rarer complex ones that mix many inputs, all arranged mostly forward rather than in loops.
summaries.intermediate: This 2022 eLife/bioRxiv study presents the first connectomic analysis of the Octopus vulgaris vertical lobe. Serial-section EM revealed new interneuron types, modulatory components, and synaptic motifs. Sensory input arrives via about 1,800,000 axons that sparsely innervate two parallel feedforward networks of simple and complex amacrine cells among 25,000,000 AMs (SAMs 89.3%; CAMs 1.6%). Each SAM receives a single input axon, implying each input neuron is represented in about 12 SAMs, whereas CAMs integrate many inputs and are proposed to supply balancing inhibition that sharpens VL output.
summaries.advanced: Cell and axon counts are reconstruction estimates for this VL sample; whole-animal completeness is not claimed. The strictly feedforward associative-learning interpretation is anatomical. CAM fraction (1.6%) plus SAM (89.3%) leaves other AM types undescribed in the abstract percentages. Comparisons to other animals’ associative circuits are qualitative. Dataset tag DS21 octopus matches the organism.

plain_language_summary: Octopuses learn using a brain region called the vertical lobe. This map shows two kinds of tiny cells: many simple ones that each listen to a single incoming fiber, and rarer complex ones that mix many inputs, all arranged mostly forward rather than in loops.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM can reveal nanometre-scale 3D structure, but conventional throughput has limited sample size and number, even as acquisition speed is now leaping toward organs and small organisms.
ocar.challenge: Faster imaging creates or worsens bottlenecks in sample preparation, image analysis, and data management even as automatic segmentation and server-based annotation improve.
ocar.action: Kievits and colleagues review methodological innovations that increase volume-EM throughput and discuss implications across the rest of the pipeline.
ocar.resolution: The review maps emerging high-throughput methods and remaining challenges, arguing that stunning progress in analysis still leaves preparation and data management as stressed bottlenecks.
ocar.future_work: Balancing acquisition speed with preparation quality, storage, and analysis capacity is the systems problem the review sets for the next generation of volume-EM projects.

summaries.beginner: New electron-microscope methods can scan much larger pieces of tissue much faster. This review explains those speedups and warns that preparing samples and storing the pictures can become the new bottlenecks.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Journal of Microscopy (2022), this review discusses how innovations in volume electron microscopy are expanding structural imaging toward whole organs and small organisms. The authors describe emerging methods for increasing throughput and the resulting stress on sample preparation, image analysis, and data management. They note stunning progress in automatic segmentation and server-based annotation while arguing that several pipeline challenges remain. The piece is a methods-prospectus for volume EM rather than a new dataset.
summaries.advanced: As a review, claims about “revolution” and remaining bottlenecks are expert synthesis, not new measurements. Throughput comparisons across modalities are discussed conceptually in the abstract without a single table of metrics. Analysis progress is credited largely to automatic segmentation and annotation tools, which still require proofreading not quantified here. The paper’s value is agenda-setting for labs planning large volume-EM projects.

plain_language_summary: New electron-microscope methods can scan much larger pieces of tissue much faster. This review explains those speedups and warns that preparing samples and storing the pictures can become the new bottlenecks.

ocar.opportunity: Nanometer EM provides the raw imagery for multi-layer maps of cell type, subcellular identity, and connectivity, but annotating those layers on segmented volumes is label-hungry.
ocar.challenge: Supervised classifiers need many labels, and many neurites in a volume are truncated, so cell type must often be inferred from short fragments.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald and colleagues introduce SegCLR, self-supervised contrastive learning on 3D imagery plus segmentations, applied to human and mouse cortical volumes.
ocar.resolution: SegCLR classified cellular subcompartments accurately and matched supervised performance with 400-fold fewer labels. Cell types could be inferred from fragments as small as 10 µm. The method enabled exploration of layer-5 pyramidal subtypes and automated large-scale synaptic-partner analysis in mouse visual cortex.
ocar.future_work: Deploying SegCLR embeddings as standard annotation layers on new EM volumes would test the 400-fold label reduction outside the human/mouse cortex volumes used here.

summaries.beginner: Once computers have outlined cells in a brain volume, this method learns useful descriptions of those pieces without many labels. It can guess what part of a cell you are looking at, and even the cell’s type from a short snippet.
summaries.intermediate: This 2022/2023 study presents SegCLR, segmentation-guided contrastive learning of representations from 3D EM imagery and segmentations. Applied to human and mouse cortical volumes, it classified cellular subcompartments and reached supervised-level performance with 400-fold fewer labeled examples. Cell types could be inferred from fragments as small as 10 µm, helping volumes where neurites are truncated at boundaries. Applications include exploring layer-5 pyramidal subtypes and automated synaptic-partner analysis in mouse visual cortex.
summaries.advanced: The catalog lists journal as bioRxiv (2022) while the DOI is a Nature Methods paper; pedagogical text should follow the row (bioRxiv 2022) without inventing a 2023 venue. The 400-fold label reduction and 10 µm fragment claim are the headline efficiencies; class sets and accuracy numbers are not in the abstract. Human and mouse cortex demonstrations may not transfer to invertebrate neuropil. Partner analysis quality depends on underlying segmentation and synapse detection.

plain_language_summary: Once computers have outlined cells in a brain volume, this method learns useful descriptions of those pieces without many labels. It can guess what part of a cell you are looking at, and even the cell’s type from a short snippet.

ocar.opportunity: New EM reconstructions contain tens of thousands of neurons and tens of millions of connections and interest non-specialists, so publication of files is not enough.
ocar.challenge: Past reconstructions could be downloaded by experts; larger graphs need a public, easy, high-performance analysis stack, plus honesty about reconstruction quality, and hosting has real costs.
ocar.action: Plaza and colleagues introduce neuPrint: a web interface for typical biological queries in the browser, programmer APIs, reconstruction-quality tools, and a neo4j/Cypher graph backend.
ocar.resolution: neuPrint made large connectomes queryable worldwide. The authors also report an open-science experiment: many readers went straight to the data after the preprint, implying data-only interest and that public hosting speeds propagation by months—while imposing substantial extra cost.
ocar.future_work: Sustaining public query hosting as connectomes grow, and designing data-only papers that the community will cite, are the socio-technical problems the paper surfaces.

summaries.beginner: A giant fly wiring diagram is useless if only a few experts can open it. neuPrint is a website and programming toolkit that lets anyone ask who connects to whom, while also showing how complete the map is.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2022), this paper presents neuPrint as an open-access analysis system for EM connectomes. A web interface supports typical biological queries from a browser; APIs support complex or high-volume queries; a neo4j graph store provides Cypher access and quality-assessment features. The authors argue this design will extend to larger future databases. They also describe preprint-driven data use, finding that many readers queried data immediately and that keeping data online adds substantial cost to connectomics research.
summaries.advanced: Performance claims are qualitative (“high performance for typical queries”) without latency numbers in the abstract. The open-science observations (preprint vs formal publication little affecting downloads) are a meta-result about this resource, not a randomized communication study. Graph modeling in neo4j may need revisiting for still-larger connectomes, as the authors themselves anticipate. A 2020 bioRxiv neuPrint paper is a closely related earlier version.

plain_language_summary: A giant fly wiring diagram is useless if only a few experts can open it. neuPrint is a website and programming toolkit that lets anyone ask who connects to whom, while also showing how complete the map is.

ocar.opportunity: Physiology can be measured in many animals, but synaptic structure is usually low-throughput EM, blocking studies of how circuit structure co-varies with behavior across individuals.
ocar.challenge: EM yields dense connectomes slowly; light microscopy is high-throughput but historically lacked synaptic resolution.
ocar.action: Lillvis and colleagues combined tissue expansion with light-sheet microscopy (ExLLSM) and a high-throughput analysis pipeline to reconstruct selected Drosophila circuits at single-synapse resolution with molecular contrast, comparing counts to EM and relating structure to function and behavior across animals.
ocar.resolution: Synaptic counts were similar to EM. The method enabled comparison of synaptic connectivity across sex and experience and correlation of structural connectivity, functional connectivity, and behavior. It is presented as filling the gap between dense EM and molecular LM.
ocar.future_work: Applying ExLLSM population measurements to more circuits and species would test how generally expansion light-sheet can substitute for EM when the question is variability rather than a single dense map.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes give precise connection maps but slowly; light microscopes are faster but usually blur synapses. Expanding the tissue and using a light-sheet microscope let this team count synapses in many fruit flies and compare wiring with behavior.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2022), this study presents an ExLLSM pipeline—tissue expansion plus light-sheet microscopy—for rapid reconstruction of selected Drosophila circuits at single-synapse resolution with molecular contrast. Synaptic counts were similar to those from EM. The approach allowed connectivity to be compared across sex and experience and to be correlated with functional connectivity and behavior. The authors argue this bridges dense, low-throughput EM and high-throughput light microscopy.
summaries.advanced: “Similar” synaptic counts to EM is the validation claim; the abstract does not report a correlation coefficient. Selected circuits, not whole-brain dense reconstruction, are in scope. Expansion can introduce distortions; the abstract does not discuss residual registration error. The method’s niche is population-scale selected circuits, not replacing EM connectomes.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes give precise connection maps but slowly; light microscopes are faster but usually blur synapses. Expanding the tissue and using a light-sheet microscope let this team count synapses in many fruit flies and compare wiring with behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM segmentation has improved but still needs costly human proofreading, especially along thin axons, before many connectomic analyses are trustworthy.
ocar.challenge: Error correction at cortical scale is expensive if it remains manual, so an automated tracer that can follow neurites in EM and repair state-of-the-art segmentations is needed.
ocar.action: Schmidt and colleagues introduce RoboEM, an AI self-steering 3D flight system trained to navigate neurites from EM alone, and use it to improve automated segmentations and to replace human proofreading on more complex analyses.
ocar.resolution: RoboEM substantially improved state-of-the-art segmentations. Computational annotation cost for cortical connectomes is reported as about 400-fold lower than manual error correction.
ocar.future_work: Demonstrating the same cost reduction on independent cortical volumes and on invertebrate neuropil would show whether flight tracing is a general proofreading substitute.

summaries.beginner: Thin nerve cables are easy for humans to lose in 3D electron-microscope movies. RoboEM is a computer “pilot” that flies along those cables to fix automatic traces, cutting the need for slow hand correction.
summaries.intermediate: This 2022 bioRxiv study (DOI associated with a later Nature Methods paper) presents RoboEM, an AI-based self-steering 3D flight tracer that navigates neurites using only EM imagery. Applied to automated segmentations, it substantially improved them and could replace human proofreading for more complex connectomic analyses. The authors report computational annotation cost for cortical connectomes about 400-fold lower than manual error correction. Thin axons are highlighted as the remaining pain point that flight tracing addresses.
summaries.advanced: The 400-fold cost reduction is the central quantitative claim and should be read as the authors’ comparison of computational versus manual annotation cost, not as a statement that residual biological error is 400-fold lower. “More complex connectomic analysis problems” are not enumerated in the abstract. Training to navigate from EM alone may overfit the source lab’s contrast and resolution. Split/merge leftovers after RoboEM are not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Thin nerve cables are easy for humans to lose in 3D electron-microscope movies. RoboEM is a computer “pilot” that flies along those cables to fix automatic traces, cutting the need for slow hand correction.

ocar.opportunity: The Drosophila larva has rich behavior including learning and action selection, so a complete synaptic-resolution brain connectome would ground experimental and theoretical circuit work.
ocar.challenge: Characterizing neuron types, hubs, feedforward/feedback pathways, and cross-hemisphere and brain–nerve-cord interactions at this scale had not been done for an insect brain with these cognitive-like behaviors.
ocar.action: Winding and colleagues mapped the larval Drosophila brain connectome of 3,013 neurons and 544,000 synapses and analyzed architecture, motifs, and recurrence, especially around the learning center.
ocar.resolution: They found pervasive multisensory and interhemispheric integration, high recurrence, abundant feedback from descending neurons, and novel motifs. The most recurrent circuits were the learning center’s input and output neurons. Some features resembled machine-learning architectures (multilayer shortcuts, nested recurrent loops).
ocar.future_work: The architecture is offered as a basis for future experiments and theory; testing whether the learning-center recurrence implements the hypothesized computations is the biological next step.

summaries.beginner: This team mapped every connection in a fruit-fly maggot’s brain: just over three thousand neurons and hundreds of thousands of synapses. The map shows lots of mixing of the senses and looping circuits around the learning center.
summaries.intermediate: This 2022 study (catalogued as bioRxiv; later Science) presents the synaptic-resolution connectome of a Drosophila larva brain with 3,013 neurons and 544,000 synapses. The authors characterize neuron types, hubs, feedforward and feedback pathways, and interactions across hemispheres and with the nerve cord. They report pervasive multisensory and interhemispheric integration, highly recurrent architecture, abundant descending-neuron feedback, and multiple novel motifs, with the learning center’s input and output neurons forming the most recurrent circuits. Structural features such as multilayer shortcuts and nested loops are noted as resembling powerful machine-learning architectures.
summaries.advanced: Counts (3,013 neurons; 544,000 synapses) refer to this larval brain reconstruction. Comparisons to machine-learning architectures are analogical. “Complete” insect-brain mapping here is larva, not adult. Motif novelty is relative to prior knowledge; the abstract does not list them. Functional richness (learning, value, action selection) motivates the work but is not newly measured in this abstract.

plain_language_summary: This team mapped every connection in a fruit-fly maggot’s brain: just over three thousand neurons and hundreds of thousands of synapses. The map shows lots of mixing of the senses and looping circuits around the learning center.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic connectomes omit extrasynaptic neuropeptide signaling, which is widespread and essential, so a wireless peptidergic map is needed even in C. elegans.
ocar.challenge: Building that map requires combining anatomy, single-cell gene expression, and biochemical receptor–ligand interactions rather than EM synapses alone.
ocar.action: Ripoll-Sánchez and colleagues integrated those datasets to draft a neuropeptide-signaling connectome of the C. elegans nervous system and analyzed density, cascades, autocrine foci, and topology.
ocar.resolution: The peptidergic connectome is dense, with extended cascades, autocrine foci, and a decentralized topology whose large core contains three communities with similar input patterns. Several of the most important nodes are little-studied neurons specialized for peptidergic neuromodulation. The map is offered as a prototype for neuroendocrine network organization.
ocar.future_work: Functional tests of the poorly studied peptidergic hub neurons would show whether topological importance predicts behavioral control.

summaries.beginner: Worm neurons also talk with chemical messages that do not need a synapse. This paper drafts that wireless map and finds it is densely connected, with some little-known cells sitting at important crossroads.
summaries.intermediate: This 2022 study (later Neuron) presents a draft neuropeptidergic connectome of C. elegans built by integrating single-cell anatomy and gene expression with biochemical receptor–ligand interactions. The network shows high connection density, extended signaling cascades, autocrine foci, and decentralized topology, with a large interconnected core of three communities that share similar input-connectivity patterns. Several of the most important nodes are little-studied neurons specialized for peptidergic neuromodulation. The authors propose this as a prototype for organizational principles of neuroendocrine signaling.
summaries.advanced: This is a draft inferred from expression plus receptor–ligand biochemistry, not a measured extrasynaptic contact map. High density is expected for peptide-receptor graphs and should not be compared naively to synaptic sparsity. Community structure depends on the interaction thresholding implicit in the biochemical compilation. “Little-studied” hubs are a discovery claim that invites targeted genetics.

plain_language_summary: Worm neurons also talk with chemical messages that do not need a synapse. This paper drafts that wireless map and finds it is densely connected, with some little-known cells sitting at important crossroads.

ocar.opportunity: A petascale EM fragment of human temporal cortex would let researchers inspect human synaptic circuits that have been largely inaccessible.
ocar.challenge: Preserving, cutting, imaging, and segmenting 1 mm³ of human cortex (more than 5,000 slices at ~30 nm) is a technical and computational extreme, and automated segmentation still contains split and merge errors.
ocar.action: Shapson-Coe and colleagues stained, sectioned, and imaged a rapidly preserved surgical temporal-lobe sample with multibeam SEM, then computationally rendered cells, neurites, and synapses and manually proofread 104 cells, releasing a 1.4-petabyte volume.
ocar.resolution: The volume contains 57,216 cells and 133.7 million synaptic connections. Glia outnumbered neurons 2:1; oligodendrocytes were most common; excitatory neurons were 69% of neurons and excitatory synapses 76%. Deep-layer excitatory types could be split on structure and connectivity; chandelier cells innervated one another’s axon initial segments; rare axons made up to ~20 synapses onto a target among thousands of weak inputs.
ocar.future_work: Community proofreading of the mostly automated segmentation, and cautious interpretation given epilepsy-surgery origin, are required before treating rare strong inputs as canonical human circuitry.

summaries.beginner: This preprint reconstructs a cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex from thousands of electron-microscope slices. Support cells outnumber neurons, and a few axons make unusually many contacts onto the same cell.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), this study describes multibeam SEM imaging of a 1 mm³ rapidly preserved human temporal-cortex surgical sample (more than 5,000 slices at ~30 nm). Computational reconstruction yielded 57,216 cells, hundreds of millions of neurites, and 133.7 million synapses in a 1.4-petabyte volume, with 104 cells manually proofread. Glia outnumbered neurons 2:1; oligodendrocytes were the most common cell; 69% of neurons and 76% of synapses were excitatory. The authors describe new deep-layer excitatory subsets, chandelier–chandelier initial-segment innervation, and rare multi-synaptic inputs of up to about 20 synapses.
summaries.advanced: This preprint’s 133.7 million synapses differ from the later Science paper’s about 150 million; use this row’s numbers when discussing this work_id. Automated segmentation incompleteness is explicitly acknowledged. Surgical epilepsy-access tissue is a biological caveat. Up-to-~20-synapse “powerful” inputs in the preprint versus up-to-50 in the journal article should not be blended. Proofread set (104 cells) is tiny relative to 57,216 cells.

plain_language_summary: This preprint reconstructs a cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex from thousands of electron-microscope slices. Support cells outnumber neurons, and a few axons make unusually many contacts onto the same cell.

ocar.opportunity: No complete nervous system had been reconstructed and modelled as an integrated structure–function object across synapses, morphologies, and brain regions; the C. elegans nerve ring is small enough to try.
ocar.challenge: The nerve ring had been treated as a densely packed tract, so spatial neighbourhoods, conserved versus variable wiring, and modular computation were not jointly mapped from volumetric reconstructions.
ocar.action: Brittin and colleagues integrated volumetric reconstructions from two animals with synaptic and gap-junction connectomes to build a complete structure–function model of the nerve ring.
ocar.resolution: Local neighbourhoods spatially constrain and support the synaptic connectome. A precisely wired core circuit sits in a background of variable connectivity, yielding a candidate reference core connectome. From that reference they propose a modular architecture for sensory computation, sensorimotor convergence, and brain-wide coordination.
ocar.future_work: Testing the proposed modules against activity and behavior, and adding more than two animals, would show which core connections are truly invariant.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s main nerve bundle was thought to be a packed cable of fibers. Using two complete 3D reconstructions, this paper shows internal neighborhoods, a stable core of connections, and more variable wiring around them.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2021), this study derives a multiscale structure–function model of the C. elegans nerve ring by integrating volumetric reconstructions from two animals with synaptic and gap-junction connectomes. Previously viewed as a densely packed tract, the neuropil shows internal spatial organization that constrains wiring. The connectome is not invariant: a precisely wired core is embedded in variable connectivity, and the authors propose a candidate reference core circuit. That reference supports a modular model of sensory computation and integration, sensorimotor convergence, and brain-wide coordination.
summaries.advanced: Invariance claims are from n = 2 volumetric animals plus corresponding connectomes. Core versus variable assignment depends on concordance thresholds not listed in the abstract. Gap junctions and chemical synapses are both used; their relative contribution to modules is not split out here. “Universal across phyla” is suggested for scalable robust features, which is interpretive.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s main nerve bundle was thought to be a packed cable of fibers. Using two complete 3D reconstructions, this paper shows internal neighborhoods, a stable core of connections, and more variable wiring around them.

ocar.opportunity: Accurate cortical axon reconstruction is a central remaining bottleneck in EM connectomics, but no large public cortical dataset offered dense axon ground truth for method development.
ocar.challenge: Complex axon morphology makes instance segmentation hard, and without dense labels it is difficult to train or fairly evaluate large-scale axon methods.
ocar.action: Wei and colleagues release AxonEM: two 30×30×30 µm³ EM volumes from human and mouse cortex with over 18,000 proofread axon instances, nine densely annotated training subvolumes per volume, reproduced baselines, and public code.
ocar.resolution: The dataset enables large-scale evaluation of axon instance segmentation. Two published state-of-the-art methods are reproduced as baselines on the release.
ocar.future_work: The resource is meant to foster better axon methods; beating the provided baselines on held-out axons is the intended community next step.

summaries.beginner: Tracing thin axons in cortex is one of the hardest jobs in electron-microscope mapping. This paper releases carefully checked axon labels from mouse and human cortex so other teams can train and score their tracers.
summaries.intermediate: Published at MICCAI (2021), this paper introduces the AxonEM dataset: two 30×30×30 µm³ EM volumes from human and mouse cortex with dense 3D axon instance segmentation after proofreading over 18,000 axon instances. Nine densely annotated ground-truth subvolumes are provided for training in each volume. The authors reproduce two published state-of-the-art methods as baselines and release code and data. The goal is to enable development and fair evaluation of large-scale cortical axon reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: Volumes are 30 µm cubes, so they test local axon instance segmentation, not brain-wide projection tracing. “Over 18,000” axons is a large label set for this size, but class imbalance and fragment length distributions are not in the abstract. Baselines are reproductions of two published methods; newer competitors may already exceed them. Human versus mouse domain shift is implicit in the dual release but not scored in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Tracing thin axons in cortex is one of the hardest jobs in electron-microscope mapping. This paper releases carefully checked axon labels from mouse and human cortex so other teams can train and score their tracers.

ocar.opportunity: How an entire brain’s wiring changes from birth to adulthood was unknown even in C. elegans, despite extensive knowledge of individual identified neurons.
ocar.challenge: Measuring circuit remodelling across the connectome requires full-brain reconstructions of multiple isogenic individuals at several postnatal stages.
ocar.action: Witvliet and colleagues used serial-section EM to reconstruct the full brains of eight isogenic C. elegans across postnatal stages and compared geometry, chemical synapses, and information-flow statistics.
ocar.resolution: Overall brain geometry is preserved, but chemical connectivity changes substantially: individuals differ, yet many wiring changes are consistent across maturation, altering existing strengths and adding connections. With age the brain becomes more feedforward and modular; central decision-making circuitry is maintained while sensory and motor pathways remodel.
ocar.future_work: Relating these stereotyped rewiring programs to the emergence of adult behaviors would close the developmental loop the study opens.

summaries.beginner: Researchers mapped the entire brains of eight worms at different ages. The overall layout stays the same, but many chemical connections change, and older brains look more one-way and more modular.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2021), this study reconstructs full-brain connectomes of eight isogenic C. elegans individuals across postnatal stages with serial-section EM. Overall geometry is preserved, but chemical synaptic connectivity changes on that scaffold, with both individual differences and consistent developmental wiring changes that alter connection strengths and create new connections. Developmental connectomics shows maintained central decision-making circuitry with substantial sensory and motor pathway remodelling, and a progressive shift toward more feedforward, modular organization. The work is presented as revealing principles of brain maturation.
summaries.advanced: n = 8 is large for EM whole brains but still modest for individual-difference statistics. “Isogenic” reduces genetic noise; remaining variability is developmental/experiential/technical. Feedforward and modular summaries depend on synapse thresholding and direction definitions. Geometry preserved versus connectivity changing is the key dissociation; gap junctions are not the focus of the abstract’s chemical-synapse story.

plain_language_summary: Researchers mapped the entire brains of eight worms at different ages. The overall layout stays the same, but many chemical connections change, and older brains look more one-way and more modular.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes show every synapse’s location, so in a stereotyped circuit they might also predict physiological synaptic strength—if anatomy can be parameterized with recordings.
ocar.challenge: Bridging wiring diagrams and activity maps requires subcellular, subthreshold comparisons between diverse neurons and synapses in the same stereotyped network.
ocar.action: Liu and colleagues compared anatomy and physiology of diverse neurons and synapses in a stereotyped Drosophila olfactory network, then fit biophysical models relating synapse density and location to somatic postsynaptic potentials.
ocar.resolution: Synapse density and location jointly predicted the amplitude of the somatic PSP evoked by a single presynaptic spike. Models predicted that axonal and dendritic electrical compartmentalization balances independent and interacting computations.
ocar.future_work: Testing whether the same density-plus-location rule predicts strengths in less stereotyped circuits would show how far this anatomy-to-weight mapping generalizes.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram counts contacts, but that is not automatically the same as connection strength. In a fly smell circuit, this team shows that how many synapses there are and where they sit on the cell together predict the size of the electrical response.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), this study compares subcellular anatomy and subthreshold physiology in a stereotyped Drosophila olfactory network. Synapse density and location jointly predict the amplitude of the somatic postsynaptic potential evoked by a single presynaptic spike. Biophysical models fit to the data predict that electrical compartmentalization lets axonal and dendritic arbors balance independent versus interacting computations. The authors frame the result as beginning to fill the gap between connectivity maps and activity maps.
summaries.advanced: The result is for a stereotyped olfactory network; the abstract does not claim a universal synapse-count-to-weight law (a related 2020 paper argues counts approximate area in Drosophila more generally). Predictions are of somatic PSP amplitude, not of computational role directly. Compartmentalization conclusions come from models fit to these data. Stereotypy of the chosen circuit is what makes paired anatomy–physiology tractable.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram counts contacts, but that is not automatically the same as connection strength. In a fly smell circuit, this team shows that how many synapses there are and where they sit on the cell together predict the size of the electrical response.

ocar.opportunity: Relating neurons’ visual responses to the circuits that shape them requires a large volume in which physiology and EM reconstructions coexist.
ocar.challenge: Co-registering dense calcium imaging of tens of thousands of neurons with a millimeter-scale EM volume containing hundreds of thousands of cells and hundreds of millions of synapses, then proofreading enough neurons to recover complete dendrites and inter-areal axons, is a community-scale resource problem.
ocar.action: The MICrONS consortium recorded activity from approximately 75,000 neurons in mouse VISp, VISrl, VISal, and VISlm during natural movies and synthetic stimuli, co-registered the data with an EM volume of more than 200,000 cells and 0.5 billion synapses, and proofread a subset with complete dendritic trees and local plus inter-areal axons.
ocar.resolution: The dataset is released as an open resource with retrieval tools. Accompanying papers use it for cortical cell-type structure, a detailed column connectivity diagram with cell-type-specific inhibitory motifs, and principles of excitatory wiring within and across areas.
ocar.future_work: The resource is explicitly for the community; linking remaining un-proofread cells to function, and testing the reported wiring principles in other individuals, are the follow-ons.

summaries.beginner: Scientists recorded how tens of thousands of mouse visual-cortex cells respond to movies, then mapped the same chunk of brain in an electron microscope. The combined public dataset lets others ask how a cell’s job relates to its connections.
summaries.intermediate: This 2021 bioRxiv resource (later Nature) presents functional connectomics spanning multiple mouse visual areas. Calcium imaging of approximately 75,000 neurons in VISp, VISrl, VISal, and VISlm in an awake mouse viewing natural movies and synthetic stimuli was co-registered with an EM volume containing more than 200,000 cells and 0.5 billion synapses. Proofreading of a subset yielded complete dendritic trees and local plus inter-areal axons that can map up to thousands of cell-to-cell connections per neuron. Accompanying papers report cell-type structure, inhibitory motifs, and excitatory wiring principles within and across areas.
summaries.advanced: Functional n ≈ 75,000 versus EM >200,000 cells means many reconstructed cells lack matched activity. “Up to thousands” of connections per neuron is an upper range for proofread cells, not a mean. One mouse, four visual areas. Natural-movie and synthetic-stimulus battery defines the functional space; other behaviors are outside this release. Companion paper numbering in the abstract indicates this is a flagship resource, not a single result.

plain_language_summary: Scientists recorded how tens of thousands of mouse visual-cortex cells respond to movies, then mapped the same chunk of brain in an electron microscope. The combined public dataset lets others ask how a cell’s job relates to its connections.
