ocar.opportunity: Dopaminergic axons strongly influence behavior and addiction, but how they communicate in nucleus accumbens and how that communication changes after cocaine is poorly understood at EM resolution.
ocar.challenge: DA varicosities may not form classical synapses, and detecting remodeling after drug exposure requires cell-type-specific labeling plus large-volume serial EM before and after cocaine.
ocar.action: Wildenberg and colleagues used cell-type-specific labeling and large-volume serial EM to examine DA connections in mouse NAc before and after cocaine, scoring varicosity contents, synapses, spinules, branching, and mitochondria.
ocar.resolution: Varicosity types based on vesicle content appeared non-randomly ordered along axons. Classical synapses were rare (<2%, 6/410), while spinule-like structures were more common (15%, 61/410). After cocaine, DA axons were extensively branched, formed mitochondria-filled bulbs surrounded by elaborated glia, and mitochondrial lengths increased ~2.2-fold in DA axons and NAc spiny dendrites only.
ocar.future_work: Because DA transmission in NAc looks largely non-synaptic here, models of cocaine plasticity should focus on axonal rearrangement and mitochondria rather than synapse counts alone.

summaries.beginner: Dopamine fibers in a reward region of mouse brain rarely make classic synapses. After a brief cocaine exposure, those fibers branch more, form bulb-like endings packed with mitochondria, and the mitochondria themselves get longer.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2021), this study combines cell-type-specific labeling with large-volume serial EM of dopaminergic axons in mouse nucleus accumbens before and after cocaine. Individual DA axons contain multiple varicosity types by vesicle content, apparently non-randomly ordered. Varicosities rarely make specific synapses (6/410, <2%) but more often form spinule-like structures (61/410, 15%). Days after brief cocaine, DA axons were extensively branched, formed mitochondria-filled blind-ended bulbs surrounded by elaborated glia, and mitochondrial lengths increased about 2.2 times in DA axons and NAc spiny dendrites only. The authors conclude that DA transmission in NAc is unlikely to be classical-synaptic and that cocaine’s anatomical plasticity is largely axonal and mitochondrial.
summaries.advanced: Synapse rarity (6/410) is for scored varicosities in this sample, not a brain-wide DA census. Cocaine effects are days after brief exposure; chronic models may differ. Mitochondrial lengthening is reported only in DA axons and spiny dendrites, a specificity claim that depends on the compared cell classes. Non-synaptic communication is an inference from ultrastructure (varicosities, spinules), not a measured extrasynaptic dopamine time course.

plain_language_summary: Dopamine fibers in a reward region of mouse brain rarely make classic synapses. After a brief cocaine exposure, those fibers branch more, form bulb-like endings packed with mitochondria, and the mitochondria themselves get longer.

ocar.opportunity: 3D EM has mapped invertebrate nervous systems, but applying it to large mammalian volumes requires a computational pipeline that can process petascale serial-section datasets.
ocar.challenge: Serial sections contain cracks and folds, so alignment, boundary detection, semantic labeling, synapse assignment, and agglomeration must all run as distributed cloud jobs with inspectable intermediates.
ocar.action: Macrina and colleagues built a convolutional-net pipeline for nonsmooth alignment, neuronal boundary detection, semantic voxel labeling, synapse detection and assignment, and mean-affinity agglomeration with semantic and size constraints, holding intermediates in cloud storage.
ocar.resolution: They applied the pipeline to automatically reconstruct an EM volume spanning four mouse visual cortical areas and released the code and reconstructed volume.
ocar.future_work: Automated reconstructions still require proofreading for many analyses; measuring residual merge/split rates on this four-area volume is the practical next assessment.

summaries.beginner: Mouse brains are too big for the computer pipelines that mapped tiny invertebrate nervous systems. This paper describes a cloud-scale set of neural networks that align cracked slices, find cell borders, and glue pieces into an automatic map of four visual areas.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), this study presents a computational pipeline for petascale serial-section EM reconstruction. Convolutional nets compute nonsmooth alignments across cracks and folds, detect neuronal boundaries, assign voxels to axon/dendrite/soma and other classes, and detect synapses assigned to pre- and postsynaptic segments. Segmentation uses mean-affinity agglomeration with semantic and size constraints, implemented with distributed cloud computing and viewable intermediate results. The pipeline produced an automated reconstruction of an EM volume spanning four mouse visual cortical areas, with public code and volume.
summaries.advanced: This is an automated reconstruction methods paper; it does not claim a fully proofread connectome. Four visual areas match the MICrONS-scale ambition; overlap with the functional-connectomics resource is likely but not spelled out in this abstract. Mean-affinity agglomeration parameters (semantic and size constraints) are crucial and not numerically specified here. Cloud-hosted intermediates aid debugging but are not a substitute for biological error metrics.

plain_language_summary: Mouse brains are too big for the computer pipelines that mapped tiny invertebrate nervous systems. This paper describes a cloud-scale set of neural networks that align cracked slices, find cell borders, and glue pieces into an automatic map of four visual areas.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomics needs a scalable, flexible open-source framework for semantic and instance segmentation that can exploit scarce expert labels and abundant unlabeled volumes.
ocar.challenge: Datasets vary in scale, and many tools require custom code for multi-task or semi-supervised training rather than configuration-only experiments.
ocar.action: Lin, Wei, Lichtman, and Pfister present PyTorch Connectomics (PyTC), a PyTorch toolbox for volumetric microscopy segmentation with multi-task and semi-supervised learning controlled by configuration options.
ocar.resolution: PyTC achieved the best CREMI synaptic-cleft segmentation (6.1% relative improvement over the previous best) and competitive mitochondria and neuronal-nuclei segmentation, with public code and tutorials.
ocar.future_work: Adapting the same configuration-driven setup to new tissues and modalities, as the authors invite, will test whether CREMI-level gains transfer without code changes.

summaries.beginner: This software package helps computers outline neurons, synapses, and mitochondria in 3D microscope images. It is built so labs can try new training tricks by changing settings rather than rewriting code, and it posted a top score on a synapse-finding contest.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on arXiv (2021), this paper presents PyTorch Connectomics, an open-source deep-learning framework for semantic and instance segmentation of volumetric microscopy. It targets connectomic reconstruction of neurons, synapses, and organelles, supporting multi-task and semi-supervised learning to exploit expensive labels and unlabeled data. Those modes are enabled by configuration rather than custom code and are intended to transfer to other 2D/3D segmentation tasks. Quantitatively, the framework achieved the best CREMI synaptic-cleft result (6.1% relative improvement over the prior best) and competitive mitochondria and neuronal-nuclei segmentation.
summaries.advanced: CREMI cleft win is the headline number; mitochondria and nuclei are only “competitive.” Relative 6.1% improvement needs the CREMI metric definition (not restated in the abstract). Configuration-only flexibility is a software claim, not a guarantee of SOTA on every new volume. The framework is 2D/3D general, but all reported scores are connectomics EM tasks.

plain_language_summary: This software package helps computers outline neurons, synapses, and mitochondria in 3D microscope images. It is built so labs can try new training tricks by changing settings rather than rewriting code, and it posted a top score on a synapse-finding contest.

ocar.opportunity: Average connectivity of cortical interneuron classes is increasingly known, but the synaptic-resolution distribution of chandelier-cell input onto pyramidal axon initial segments—and its functional meaning—was not mapped in visual cortex.
ocar.challenge: Relating synapse number to target-cell structure, comparing variability with perisomatic inhibition, and linking circuit-wide chandelier activity to behavior requires combining dense EM, biophysical simulation, and cell-type-specific imaging.
ocar.action: Schneider-Mizell and colleagues used large-scale EM to map complete chandelier input onto 153 layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in mouse visual cortex, simulated the observed axo-axonic pattern, and imaged chandelier population activity in awake mice.
ocar.resolution: Chandelier synapse number was highly variable and correlated with structural features of the target, more variable than perisomatic inhibition. Simulations indicated the pattern is particularly effective when excitation and inhibition are co-active. In vivo, chandelier cells were highly correlated with each other and with pupil dilation, a proxy for arousal, suggesting a circuit-wide signal whose strength is adjusted to target properties.
ocar.future_work: Whether the same target-adjusted, arousal-locked chandelier broadcast exists outside L2/3 visual cortex is the natural generalization test.

summaries.beginner: Chandelier cells put inhibitory contacts on the start of a pyramid cell’s output wire. This study maps those contacts onto many cells, finds the number varies a lot, and shows chandelier cells in awake mice fire together and track arousal.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2021), this study maps complete chandelier-cell synaptic input onto 153 pyramidal neurons in layer 2/3 of mouse visual cortex using dense EM. Synapse number varied widely and correlated with structural features of the target, exceeding the variability of perisomatic inhibition. Biophysical simulations indicate the observed axo-axonic pattern is particularly effective at controlling excitatory output when excitation and inhibition are co-active. Cell-type-specific calcium imaging in awake animals showed highly correlated chandelier activity that tracked pupil dilation, suggesting a circuit-wide arousal-related signal scaled to target properties.
summaries.advanced: n = 153 pyramids in L2/3 visual cortex of the EM volume; other layers/areas are untested here. Correlation with target structural features is reported without listing which features in the abstract. Pupil dilation is a proxy for arousal, not a causal manipulation of chandelier cells. Co-active E/I effectiveness is a simulation result. High pairwise correlation among chandelier cells supports a broadcast, but does not prove identical input onto every pyramid.

plain_language_summary: Chandelier cells put inhibitory contacts on the start of a pyramid cell’s output wire. This study maps those contacts onto many cells, finds the number varies a lot, and shows chandelier cells in awake mice fire together and track arousal.

ocar.opportunity: The circuits that generate fly behavior were largely unknown at synapse resolution for a large fraction of the central brain.
ocar.challenge: Preparing, imaging, aligning, segmenting, detecting synapses, and proofreading a dataset of this size required new procedures, as did defining cell types and giving the community usable access and genetic links.
ocar.action: Scheffer and colleagues summarize those improved methods and present circuitry for most of the adult Drosophila central brain, with public data, simplified access, and procedures linking reconstructed neurons to genetic reagents.
ocar.resolution: They define cell types, refine computational compartments, provide an atlas of many novel examples, and examine connection-strength distributions, motifs at several scales, electrical consequences of compartmentalization, and evidence that packing density is an important evolutionary criterion.
ocar.future_work: Linking the released central-brain circuits to behavior with the associated genetic reagents is the intended biological use of the resource.

summaries.beginner: This paper maps a large part of the adult fruit-fly central brain: the cells, their chemical connections, and names for many cell types. The data are public, with recipes to match cells to genetic tools.
summaries.intermediate: This 2020 study (catalogued as bioRxiv; later eLife) presents a connectome and analysis of a large fraction of the adult Drosophila central brain. Improved methods cover preparation, imaging, alignment, segmentation, synapse finding, and proofreading. The authors define cell types, refine computational compartments, and provide an exhaustive atlas of cell examples and types, many novel, with detailed neuron-and-synapse circuits for most of the central brain. Biological analyses include connection-strength distributions, motifs at different scales, electrical consequences of compartmentalization, and evidence that maximizing packing density shaped the fly brain. Data are public with simplified access and links to genetic reagents.
summaries.advanced: This resource overlaps the “hemibrain” reconstruction; a companion 2020 bioRxiv from FlyEM/Google is the closely related methods-and-data dump. “Most of the central brain” is not a whole-brain connectome (optic lobes and VNC are out of scope). Packing-density evolution is an interpretive finding from the reconstructions. Connection-strength distributions depend on synapse proofreading completeness not quantified in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: This paper maps a large part of the adult fruit-fly central brain: the cells, their chemical connections, and names for many cell types. The data are public, with recipes to match cells to genetic tools.

ocar.opportunity: Complete circuits were known only for animals with hundreds of neurons or for selected circuits in larger brains; a large fraction of a complex central brain at synapse resolution was missing.
ocar.challenge: Scale required new preparation, imaging, alignment, segmentation, synapse detection, and proofreading, plus connectivity-aware cell typing and simplified public access to an evolving dataset.
ocar.action: The FlyEM project at Janelia and Google collaborators present the complete circuitry of a large fraction of the adult Drosophila central brain (the hemibrain), with a website designed for experts and non-experts.
ocar.resolution: Deliverables include better computational-compartment definitions, an atlas of cell examples and types (many novel), detailed circuits for most of the central brain, and statistical exploration of compartments and the brain as a whole, reducing the effort to identify partners and match genetic reagents.
ocar.future_work: The authors announce companion papers with deeper analysis of the hemibrain, central complex, and mushroom body as the interpretive follow-ons to this methods-and-access release.

summaries.beginner: A Janelia–Google team mapped a large chunk of an adult fruit-fly brain in enough detail to see individual connections. They put the map online so anyone can ask which cells talk to which.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this FlyEM/Google paper presents a connectome of a large fraction of the adult Drosophila central brain. New methods span sample preparation through proofreading, define cell types from connectivity as well as morphology, and simplify access to a large evolving dataset. From the data the authors derive computational compartments and their connections, an exhaustive cell atlas including novel types, detailed circuits for most of the central brain, and compartment- and brain-wide statistics. Public web resources are designed for both experts and casual users, lowering the effort to find synaptic partners and genetic reagents.
summaries.advanced: This is the hemibrain resource announcement; later eLife/Nature papers analyze subcircuits in more depth. “Complete circuitry of a large fraction” still excludes much of the optic lobes and the rest of the animal. Cell typing from connectivity plus morphology is a methodological claim that later comparative work (FlyWire vs hemibrain) would stress-test. Companion papers promised “in the next few weeks” situate this as a living data release.

plain_language_summary: A Janelia–Google team mapped a large chunk of an adult fruit-fly brain in enough detail to see individual connections. They put the map online so anyone can ask which cells talk to which.

ocar.opportunity: The insect central complex supports directed locomotion, sleep, and context-dependent navigation via recurrent dynamics, but a complete synaptic connectome of the Drosophila CX was lacking.
ocar.challenge: Flexible, long-timescale behaviors are thought to engage deep recurrent networks that are hard to study without a full parts list of neurons, sensory/motor pathways, and motifs.
ocar.action: Hulse and colleagues describe the first complete EM connectome of the Drosophila CX, identifying neuron types, pathways, and network motifs, and relating them to head-direction, attractor, and vector-navigation computations.
ocar.resolution: They report new CX neuron types, novel sensory and motor pathways, and motifs likely enabling head-direction extraction, attractor maintenance, and vector-based navigation, plus numerous pathways that could select CX-driven behaviors by context and internal state. The connectome is offered as a blueprint for network dynamics of sleep, flexible navigation, and state-dependent action selection.
ocar.future_work: Physiology and modeling constrained by these motifs are needed to test which of the proposed head-direction and action-selection pathways actually implement those computations.

summaries.beginner: The fly’s central complex helps it tell direction, sleep, and choose actions. This paper maps every cell and connection in that region and points to repeating wiring patterns that could keep a sense of heading and pick what to do next.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this study presents the first complete EM-based connectome of the Drosophila central complex, including all its neurons and circuits at synaptic resolution. The authors identify new CX neuron types, novel sensory and motor pathways, and network motifs thought to extract head direction, maintain it with attractor dynamics, and combine it with other sensorimotor information for vector-based navigation. They also catalog pathways that may allow context- and state-dependent selection of CX-driven behaviors. The CX connectome is framed as a comprehensive blueprint for dynamics underlying sleep, flexible navigation, and action selection.
summaries.advanced: “Complete” is for the CX in this EM volume, not the whole brain. Motifs are interpreted as “likely” enabling attractor and vector computations; those functions are not re-measured here. New neuron types depend on this volume’s annotation ontology. Overlap with the hemibrain CX analysis promised in companion papers should be expected.

plain_language_summary: The fly’s central complex helps it tell direction, sleep, and choose actions. This paper maps every cell and connection in that region and points to repeating wiring patterns that could keep a sense of heading and pick what to do next.

ocar.opportunity: Joint functional and anatomical data from the same specimen would let researchers relate connectivity to activity, but even mouse-scale systems cannot yet do both comprehensively.
ocar.challenge: Smaller nervous systems can, if voltage imaging and volume EM can be applied to the same ganglion; tracing all synapses onto identified cells remains laborious.
ocar.action: Ashaber and colleagues combined voltage-sensitive dye imaging of the majority of neurons in a medicinal-leech segmental ganglion during several motor behaviors with serial block-face EM of the entire ganglion, then manually traced a critical motor neuron and all of its numerous presynaptic partners.
ocar.resolution: The VSD was sensitive enough to record subthreshold activity. Quantitative analysis of reconstructed synapses revealed spatial clustering of synapses from functionally synchronized cell assemblies. All data are public.
ocar.future_work: Extending manual partner tracing beyond the proof-of-concept motor neuron would test whether synapse clustering by functional assembly is general in this ganglion.

summaries.beginner: In a leech nerve ganglion, researchers first watched most cells’ electrical activity during movement, then mapped the same ganglion in an electron microscope. Contacts from cells that had fired together tended to sit near each other on a motor neuron.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this study obtains joint functional and anatomical data from a medicinal-leech segmental ganglion by combining voltage-sensitive dye imaging with serial block-face EM. VSD imaging recorded the majority of neurons during several motor behaviors with sensitivity to subthreshold activity; SBEM then imaged the entire ganglion. As a proof of concept, the authors manually traced a critical motor neuron and identified all of its numerous presynaptic partners. Synapses from functionally synchronized assemblies were spatially clustered. Data are publicly available.
summaries.advanced: The catalog organism/dataset fields (mouse; Platynereis) conflict with the abstract’s medicinal leech; the narrative follows the abstract. Only one motor neuron is fully partner-traced, so clustering is a proof of concept. “Majority of the neurons” is not a count. Journal metadata is empty in the input row; year 2020 and bioRxiv-style DOI are used. Functional assemblies are defined from VSD during motor behaviors, which may not match other states.

plain_language_summary: In a leech nerve ganglion, researchers first watched most cells’ electrical activity during movement, then mapped the same ganglion in an electron microscope. Contacts from cells that had fired together tended to sit near each other on a motor neuron.

ocar.opportunity: How embryonic partners find each other and set appropriate connection numbers is poorly understood, and a tractable system is the Drosophila embryonic nerve cord.
ocar.challenge: Partner identity, axon-terminal location, and activity are entangled, so they must be dissociated experimentally and scored at EM synaptic resolution with functional and behavioral readouts.
ocar.action: Valdes-Aleman and colleagues combined EM reconstruction, functional imaging, and behavior after shifting partners to ectopic locations or silencing them, then quantified connection numbers, E/I balance, and behavior.
ocar.resolution: Postsynaptic cells still found and connected to shifted or silenced presynaptic partners. However, orderly positioning by positional cues and synaptic activity were required for appropriate connection numbers between specific partners, appropriate E/I balance, and appropriate functional connectivity and behavior.
ocar.future_work: Identifying the positional cues and activity-dependent rules that set those numbers, rather than partner choice per se, is the mechanistic next step this study isolates.

summaries.beginner: Developing fly neurons can still find their correct partners even if those partners are moved or silenced. Getting the right number of connections, and the right mix of excitation and inhibition, does require cells to sit in the right place and to be electrically active.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Neuron (2020), this study uses EM reconstruction, activity imaging, and behavior in the Drosophila embryonic nerve cord to separate partner identity, location, and activity during circuit assembly. Postsynaptic neurons could find and connect to presynaptic partners shifted to ectopic locations or silenced. Orderly axon-terminal positioning by positional cues, and synaptic activity, were nevertheless required for appropriate connection numbers, excitatory/inhibitory balance, functional connectivity, and behavior. The work resolves partner choice versus quantitative matching at synaptic resolution.
summaries.advanced: “Find and connect” despite ectopic shift or silencing is a qualitative capacity claim; residual targeting error rates are not in the abstract. Quantitative matching (counts, E/I, behavior) is where location and activity matter. The system is embryonic nerve cord, not adult brain. Combined EM, imaging, and behavior is a strength; each perturbation class (shift vs silence) may affect counts through different mechanisms not separated numerically here.

plain_language_summary: Developing fly neurons can still find their correct partners even if those partners are moved or silenced. Getting the right number of connections, and the right mix of excitation and inhibition, does require cells to sit in the right place and to be electrically active.

ocar.opportunity: A complete inventory of olfactory projection neurons from antennal lobe to higher centers in an adult brain would provide synaptic-resolution holotypes for both famous and unknown cell types.
ocar.challenge: Light-level catalogs undercounted PNs, and left–right stereotypy in cell and synapse numbers, plus non-canonical motifs in the lateral horn, had not been fully reconstructed.
ocar.action: Bates, Schlegel and colleagues reconstructed the complete set of olfactory projections in a whole adult Drosophila EM brain volume and compared hemispheres, then analyzed lateral-horn versus mushroom-body-calyx motifs.
ocar.resolution: PNs were about twice as numerous as light-level reports. Types were stereotyped but not identical in cell and synapse numbers between hemispheres. The lateral horn, main target for innate olfactory behavior, showed axo-axonic PN connectivity, local feedback/lateral inhibition onto PN axons, and convergence of non-olfactory and memory-related feedback—unlike the mushroom-body calyx configuration.
ocar.future_work: The inventory is a platform for functional studies; testing the new LH motifs physiologically is the obvious follow-on.

summaries.beginner: This team listed every second-order smell cell that carries news from a fly’s antennal lobe to higher brain areas. There were about twice as many as older light-microscope counts, and the two brain sides were similar but not identical.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this study reconstructs a complete inventory of olfactory projection neurons connecting the adult Drosophila antennal lobe to higher-order regions in a whole-brain EM volume. Projection neurons were approximately twice as numerous as in light-level studies; cell types were stereotyped but not identical in cell and synapse numbers between hemispheres. The lateral horn is the main target and contains motifs including axo-axonic PN connectivity, feedback and lateral inhibition of PN axons by local neurons, and convergence of non-olfactory and memory-related feedback onto LH neurons—distinct from mushroom-body calyx architecture. The catalog provides synaptic-resolution holotypes for known and new types.
summaries.advanced: “Approximately twice as numerous” is relative to prior light-level reports, which may have missed types rather than undercounted matched types. Hemispheric non-identity is expected biological/technical noise; the abstract does not give a coefficient of variation. LH versus calyx motif contrast is anatomical. Completeness is for olfactory PNs in this brain, not all AL outputs.

plain_language_summary: This team listed every second-order smell cell that carries news from a fly’s antennal lobe to higher brain areas. There were about twice as many as older light-microscope counts, and the two brain sides were similar but not identical.

ocar.opportunity: Temperature and humidity are critical for fly survival, but the higher-order thermosensory and hygrosensory neurons downstream of antennal VP glomeruli were incompletely known.
ocar.challenge: Two VP glomeruli were unrecognized, and a comprehensive synaptic map of the mushroom-body lateral accessory calyx and other third-order partners required a whole-brain EM volume.
ocar.action: Marin and colleagues used a whole adult brain EM volume to identify VP glomeruli and their projection neurons, fully reconstruct neurons downstream of heating- and cooling-responsive VP PNs in the lACA, and survey strong partners of VP PNs across the protocerebrum.
ocar.resolution: They report two new VP glomeruli, the first complete set of thermo/hygrosensory PNs, and a first lACA connectome: a few Kenyon cells are purely thermosensory while most mix olfactory and thermo/hygro input. The lACA is a general thermosensory hub, including DN1 pacemakers linking to the accessory medulla. A descending neuron mainly downstream of dry-responsive VP PNs sits only two synapses from nerve-cord motor neurons.
ocar.future_work: Functional tests of the lACA hub, DN1 temperature-entrainment path, and the two-synapse dry-to-descending route would confirm the proposed roles.

summaries.beginner: Flies sense heat, cold, and moisture with specific antennal cells. This map follows those signals into the brain, finds two previously unknown input glomeruli, and shows a short path from “dry” sensors toward movement-controlling cells.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this study uses a whole adult Drosophila EM brain to map thermosensory and hygrosensory circuits from ventroposterior antennal-lobe glomeruli. Two new VP glomeruli are identified, along with projection neurons relaying VP information to mushroom body and lateral horn. A comprehensive lACA connectome downstream of heating- and cooling-responsive PNs shows some Kenyon cells receiving solely thermosensory input while most also receive olfactory and thermo/hygro input in the main calyx. Several lACA-associated neuron classes form a local network with outputs to other neuropils, including DN1 pacemakers to the accessory medulla. A descending neuron receiving mainly dry-responsive VP input implies as few as two synapses from hygrosensory afferents to nerve-cord motor neurons.
summaries.advanced: “First complete set” of thermo/hygrosensory PNs is relative to this EM volume’s annotations. The two-synapse dry pathway is a shortest-path anatomical claim, not a demonstrated reflex arc. Mixed versus pure Kenyon-cell input depends on synapse thresholds. Circadian interpretation of DN1–lACA links is by known pacemaker identity, not new clock recordings here.

plain_language_summary: Flies sense heat, cold, and moisture with specific antennal cells. This map follows those signals into the brain, finds two previously unknown input glomeruli, and shows a short path from “dry” sensors toward movement-controlling cells.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain connectomes with 100,000+ neurons were becoming feasible, but proofreading at that scale would take many person-years unless it could be distributed globally.
ocar.challenge: Huge EM volumes require a computational and social system that lets people anywhere correct 3D reconstructions, tracks edits for quality and incentives, and keeps discoveries open.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald and colleagues present FlyWire, a browser-based community for collaborative editing of a spatially chunked supervoxel graph of a Drosophila brain, with programmatic access to edit history.
ocar.resolution: Distributed proofreading became possible worldwide. Open community structure is argued to recruit more participants and accelerate discovery via required sharing. The authors demonstrate circuit analysis by reconstructing the connectome of mechanosensory neurons.
ocar.future_work: The same social-and-software pattern is intended to scale to still-larger brains; maintaining incentive systems and accuracy estimates from the edit history is ongoing infrastructure work.

summaries.beginner: Correcting a whole fly-brain map is too much for one lab. FlyWire is a website where people around the world can fix 3D cell traces together, and the history of those fixes is recorded.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Methods (2020/2021), this paper presents FlyWire, an online community and platform for proofreading EM connectome data of a Drosophila brain. Browser-based 3D interactive segmentation via collaborative editing of a spatially chunked supervoxel graph distributes proofreading globally. Edit-history information can be used to estimate accuracy or build incentives. An open community is argued to accelerate both proofreading and discovery through mandatory information sharing. The authors demonstrate the platform by reconstructing and analyzing mechanosensory-neuron connectivity.
summaries.advanced: This is a platform paper; whole-brain completeness is a later FlyWire consortium achievement, not this abstract’s result. The mechanosensory demonstration is a circuit-sized proof of capability. Accuracy estimation from edit history is enabled, not reported as a final error rate here. Social scaling claims (more participants, faster discovery) are design arguments plus early experience.

plain_language_summary: Correcting a whole fly-brain map is too much for one lab. FlyWire is a website where people around the world can fix 3D cell traces together, and the history of those fixes is recorded.

ocar.opportunity: The hemibrain connectome covers most of the Drosophila central brain, making a complete description of first-, second-, and lateral-horn-associated third-order olfactory neurons finally possible.
ocar.challenge: Turning a huge connectome graph into layered information flow, and measuring stereotypy within versus between individuals, requires both a flow-extraction strategy and a second dataset.
ocar.action: Schlegel and colleagues fully describe the Drosophila olfactory system in the hemibrain, develop a generally applicable method to extract layered information flow to descending interneurons, and compare neurons across two brains (three hemispheres).
ocar.resolution: They map motifs including highly lateralized antennal-lobe circuits and convergence downstream of mushroom body and lateral horn. Morphology is strikingly similar across brains; connectivity correlates with morphology; neurons of the same morphological type show similar connection variability within a brain as across two brains.
ocar.future_work: The intra- versus inter-individual variability result is from two brains; more individuals would test whether type-matched connection noise is generally as large within as between animals.

summaries.beginner: Using a large fly-brain map, this paper follows smell information from the first cells to deeper layers. Comparing two brains, cell shapes look very alike, and the usual differences in connections are about as big within one brain as between two.
summaries.intermediate: This 2020 study (later eLife) uses the hemibrain connectome to provide a complete description of the Drosophila olfactory system across first-order, second-order, and lateral-horn-associated third-order neurons. A general strategy extracts information flow and layered organization from connectome graphs, mapping olfactory input to descending interneurons and identifying motifs such as highly lateralized antennal-lobe circuits and downstream convergence after mushroom body and lateral horn. Comparison across two brains (three hemispheres) shows striking morphological similarity. Connectivity correlates with morphology, and same-type neurons show similar connection variability within one brain as across two brains.
summaries.advanced: “Complete description” is relative to hemibrain coverage of the central brain, not optic lobes. The two-brain stereotypy analysis is a first quantitative assessment, as the authors state—not a large population. Similar within- versus between-brain variability could mean biological noise dominates or that matching across datasets adds comparable noise. Flow extraction is graph-theoretic; it does not measure activity.

plain_language_summary: Using a large fly-brain map, this paper follows smell information from the first cells to deeper layers. Comparing two brains, cell shapes look very alike, and the usual differences in connections are about as big within one brain as between two.

ocar.opportunity: Growing EM reconstruction datasets require server-side storage/retrieval and client-side caching so researchers can mine large volumes interactively.
ocar.challenge: Massive image pyramids and volumetric segmentations must be fetched by spatial location with stable performance, and clients must hide latency.
ocar.action: Yuan and colleagues built a module using Hadoop and HBase, pyramid storage for EM images, block storage for segmentations, a spatial-location retrieval method, and a three-level client image cache.
ocar.resolution: Retrieval of images and segments by layer is reported to achieve constant time complexity, with excellent real-time performance on large-scale data in practical tests. The server can back other software or public databases.
ocar.future_work: Sustaining constant-time spatial queries as volumes move from terascale to petascale, and supporting concurrent community editing, would be the scalability test this architecture still faces.

summaries.beginner: Huge electron-microscope brain pictures will not fit on a laptop. This software stores them on a cluster and quickly fetches just the piece you are looking at, keeping a smart cache on your computer.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Brain Science (2020), this paper presents a massive-data management and sharing module for connectome reconstruction. The server side uses Hadoop and HBase, stores EM images as resolution pyramids, stores segmentation in blocks, and retrieves images and segments by spatial location with reported constant-time complexity. The client side uses a three-level image cache to reduce latency. Theoretical analysis and practical tests are said to show excellent real-time performance, and the server can serve as a backend for other software or public databases.
summaries.advanced: “Constant time complexity” is an algorithmic claim for their spatial index; real-world constants and concurrent-user behavior are not numerically reported in the abstract. “Excellent real-time performance” is qualitative. This is infrastructure, contemporaneous with CAVE/neuPrint-style systems, without a comparative benchmark here. Pyramid plus block design is standard in large-image serving; novelty is the integrated connectomics module.

plain_language_summary: Huge electron-microscope brain pictures will not fit on a laptop. This software stores them on a cluster and quickly fetches just the piece you are looking at, keeping a smart cache on your computer.

ocar.opportunity: Fruit-fly-scale reconstructions with tens of thousands of neurons and tens of millions of synapses interest non-specialists and must be analyzed while reconstructions are still being updated.
ocar.challenge: Tools must be easy, handle large graphs, assess reconstruction quality, and support both batch and incremental updates matching modern workflows.
ocar.action: Clements and colleagues introduce neuPrint as a neo4j/Cypher graph database and analysis ecosystem, with a data model at multiple abstractions, quality tools, incremental updates, a web interface, and a programmer API.
ocar.resolution: The paper demonstrates effectiveness and efficiency through example queries, aiming to organize connectome data for biological discovery across a diverse user skill set.
ocar.future_work: Keeping incremental updates aligned with live proofreading, as reconstructions grow another order of magnitude, is the operational challenge the design anticipates.

summaries.beginner: neuPrint stores a fly wiring diagram as a graph you can query in ordinary language-like commands, in a browser or in code. It is built so the answers stay usable even while the map is still being corrected.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this paper presents neuPrint, a database and analysis ecosystem for EM connectomics. Connectome data are modeled for access at different abstractions primarily through neo4j and Cypher. The system is designed for modern reconstruction workflows, with tools to assess quality and both batch and incremental updates. A web interface and programmer API target a range of user skills. Effectiveness and efficiency are demonstrated with example queries.
summaries.advanced: This preprint is the earlier sibling of the 2022 Frontiers neuPrint paper; pedagogical claims should not treat them as independent inventions. Efficiency is shown via examples, not a benchmark suite in the abstract. Graph abstraction layers are the conceptual contribution. Incremental updates are a stated compatibility feature whose operational limits are not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: neuPrint stores a fly wiring diagram as a graph you can query in ordinary language-like commands, in a browser or in code. It is built so the answers stay usable even while the map is still being corrected.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes generally lack synaptic sign; knowing which transmitter a synapse uses would add putative excitation/inhibition and neuromodulatory identity from images alone.
ocar.challenge: Transmitter type is not traditionally scored from ultrastructure, so a predictor must work across six transmitters and be explainable enough to reveal which image features matter.
ocar.action: Eckstein and colleagues trained artificial neural networks to classify acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA, serotonin, dopamine, and octopamine from Drosophila EM micrographs at synaptic sites, developed an explainability method, and applied predictions to two connectomes.
ocar.resolution: Average accuracy was 87% per synapse and 94% per entire neuron. Explainability revealed significant ultrastructural differences among classical transmitters. Hemilineages largely express only one fast-acting transmitter. Neurons with different predicted transmitters can differ in polarization and projection targets.
ocar.future_work: Predictions remain putative signs; targeted immunohistochemistry or physiology on discordant neurons would calibrate when image-based transmitter calls fail.

summaries.beginner: Connection maps usually do not say whether a contact is excitatory or inhibitory. This computer model guesses the chemical messenger from the electron-microscope picture of the synapse, and it is quite accurate for whole fly neurons.
summaries.intermediate: This 2020 study (later Cell) shows that artificial neural networks can predict transmitter type at Drosophila synapses from EM micrographs, adding putative signs to connectomes. The network discriminates six transmitters—acetylcholine, glutamate, GABA, serotonin, dopamine, and octopamine—with average accuracy of 87% at synapses and 94% for entire neurons. An explainability method found significant ultrastructural differences among classical transmitters. Applied to two connectomes, predictions indicate that hemilineages largely express only one fast-acting transmitter and that transmitter class relates to morphological features such as polarization and projection targets.
summaries.advanced: Accuracies (87%/94%) are averages across six classes; per-class errors are not in the abstract (modulators may differ from fast transmitters). Image-based calls are putative, not biochemical assays. Hemilineage transmitter purity is a predicted-connectome finding. Explainability supports that the net uses ultrastructural cues, but those cues could correlate with bouton type rather than transmitter per se. Two-connectome application is a strength for characterizing tens of thousands of neurons by predicted transmitter.

plain_language_summary: Connection maps usually do not say whether a contact is excitatory or inhibitory. This computer model guesses the chemical messenger from the electron-microscope picture of the synapse, and it is quite accurate for whole fly neurons.

ocar.opportunity: Adding functional molecular information to dense EM reconstructions typically requires IHC, but permeabilizing thick sections destroys the ultrastructure EM needs.
ocar.challenge: A pre-embedding protocol must label cell types, enzymes, and synaptic proteins throughout hundreds of microns of tissue without detergent permeabilization, then still support 3D EM.
ocar.action: Fulton and Briggman describe a permeabilization-free en bloc immunohistochemistry protocol and perform proof-of-principle correlative two-photon and 3D EM experiments.
ocar.resolution: The protocol labeled neuronal cell types, intracellular enzymes, and synaptic proteins in sections hundreds of microns thick across multiple brain regions while retaining ultrastructural integrity, enabling correlative protein-distribution and volume-EM imaging.
ocar.future_work: Applying the protocol to full millimeter-scale EM volumes, not only proof-of-principle correlative experiments, would test penetration and contrast at connectomic scale.

summaries.beginner: Staining proteins in thick brain pieces usually requires detergents that wreck the fine structure needed for electron microscopy. This recipe stains without those detergents, so the same sample can show both glowing proteins and ultrastructure.
summaries.intermediate: This 2020 study (later eLife) presents permeabilization-free en bloc immunohistochemistry for correlative microscopy. The protocol labels neuronal cell types, intracellular enzymes, and synaptic proteins in tissue sections hundreds of microns thick, across multiple brain regions, without the detergent permeabilization that typically impairs EM ultrastructure. Ultrastructural integrity is retained. Proof-of-principle experiments combine two-photon imaging of protein distributions with 3D electron microscopy.
summaries.advanced: “Hundreds of microns” is thick for IHC but still short of many millimeter-scale EM blocks; the abstract does not claim full 1 mm³ penetration. Antibody panel and species details are not listed here (mouse and volume EM are catalog tags). Correlative experiments are proof of principle, not a released multimodal connectome. Residual compromise of extracellular space or membrane contrast is not quantified in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Staining proteins in thick brain pieces usually requires detergents that wreck the fine structure needed for electron microscopy. This recipe stains without those detergents, so the same sample can show both glowing proteins and ultrastructure.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping the networks that control limbs requires synaptic-resolution EM of the ventral nerve cord, not only the brain, and more affordable automated TEM acquisition.
ocar.challenge: Collecting and imaging thousands of serial VNC sections at high throughput was a bottleneck, as was reconstructing motor neurons and their sensory feedback at synapse resolution.
ocar.action: Maniates-Selvin and colleagues developed GridTape to combine automated serial-section collection with automated high-throughput TEM, acquired a female adult Drosophila VNC dataset, reconstructed 507 motor neurons (all those controlling legs and wings), and registered reconstructions to a standard atlas.
ocar.resolution: A class of leg sensory neurons synapses directly onto the largest-caliber motor-neuron axons on both sides of the body, a unique fast feedback pathway. Dataset, reconstructions, GridTape designs, and software are openly released to match EM to light-microscopy cells and to make large-scale TEM more accessible.
ocar.future_work: Using the sensory-to-giant-motor contacts to test fast limb feedback physiologically, and applying GridTape beyond this VNC, are the dual biological and methodological next steps.

summaries.beginner: This team invented a tape-based way to collect and photograph thousands of thin slices of a fly’s nerve cord automatically. They traced the motor neurons for legs and wings and found a shortcut from leg sensors onto the biggest motor cables.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this study presents a synapse-resolution EM dataset of an adult female Drosophila ventral nerve cord acquired with GridTape, a technology combining automated serial-section collection with automated high-throughput TEM. The authors reconstructed 507 motor neurons, including all that control the legs and wings, and registered them to a standard atlas for matching to light-microscopy data. A specific class of leg sensory neurons directly synapses onto the largest-caliber motor-neuron axons bilaterally, interpreted as a unique feedback pathway for fast limb control. Designs, software, and data are open to make large-scale EM more accessible and affordable.
summaries.advanced: 507 motor neurons include all leg- and wing-related MNs in this female VNC; other MN classes may exist beyond that “all” clause’s scope. Direct sensory-to-large-caliber-MN synapses are an anatomical motif whose latency advantage is inferred. GridTape is the methods contribution; later FANC/MANC papers provide denser VNC connectomes. Atlas registration quality is not scored in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: This team invented a tape-based way to collect and photograph thousands of thin slices of a fly’s nerve cord automatically. They traced the motor neurons for legs and wings and found a shortcut from leg sensors onto the biggest motor cables.

ocar.opportunity: Dopaminergic neurons drive learning across animals, but the upstream circuits that regulate them—and thereby learning—are poorly mapped even in the tractable larval mushroom body.
ocar.challenge: A synaptic-resolution census of all inputs to every DAN in that learning center, plus functional tests and modeling, had not been combined.
ocar.action: Eschbach, Fushiki and colleagues reconstructed the circuitry upstream of all DANs in the Drosophila larva mushroom body, mapped sensory afferents and a large feedback population from mushroom-body output neurons linking aversive and appetitive systems, and combined this with DAN physiology and circuit modeling.
ocar.resolution: DANs compare convergent feedback from aversive and appetitive systems, enabling integrated predictions that may improve future learning. Computational modeling found that the discovered feedback motifs increase model flexibility and performance on learning tasks. The study offers a detailed view of biological motifs supporting associative learning.
ocar.future_work: Whether the same aversive–appetitive feedback comparison exists in adult MB DANs would test developmental generality of the motif.

summaries.beginner: Learning signals in the fly larva come from dopamine cells, but those cells themselves need instructions. This paper maps every input to those dopamine cells, including feedback from the learning center’s outputs, and models how that looping could improve later learning.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Neuroscience (2020), this study provides a synaptic-resolution connectome of circuitry upstream of all dopaminergic neurons in the Drosophila larva mushroom body. The authors find afferent sensory pathways and a large population of neurons that feed back from mushroom-body output neurons and link aversive and appetitive memory systems. Combined functional studies and comprehensive circuit modeling indicate that DANs compare convergent aversive and appetitive feedback, computing integrated predictions that may improve future learning. Models with the discovered feedback motifs showed increased flexibility and performance on learning tasks.
summaries.advanced: “All DANs” is for this larval MB learning center, not the whole nervous system. Predictive-learning interpretation is supported by modeling plus physiology, not by a new behavioral learning assay in the abstract. Feedback linking aversive and appetitive systems is the key motif; its necessity in vivo is argued rather than lesioned circuit-by-circuit here. Adult conservation is untested in this paper.

plain_language_summary: Learning signals in the fly larva come from dopamine cells, but those cells themselves need instructions. This paper maps every input to those dopamine cells, including feedback from the learning center’s outputs, and models how that looping could improve later learning.

ocar.opportunity: Kenyon cells in the fly mushroom body were widely modeled as randomly sampling olfactory projection neurons, but that hypothesis was hard to test without synaptic-resolution PN–KC maps at scale.
ocar.challenge: Mapping large numbers of PN-to-KC synapses to compare against precisely defined random-connectivity null models requires a whole-brain EM volume.
ocar.action: Zheng and colleagues used a whole-brain adult Drosophila EM volume to map large numbers of PN–KC connections and compared the connectome to null models, then simulated discrimination performance of the observed network.
ocar.resolution: A subset of food-responsive PN types converged on individual KCs more often than expected. Overconvergence matched neurogeometry: those PN axons arborize near one another in the main calyx. Models showed input from overconvergent PNs is better discriminated than input from other types, suggesting an “associative fovea” for ethologically relevant food-odor combinations.
ocar.future_work: Testing whether food-odor mixtures that match the overconvergent PN set are learned more readily would link the anatomical fovea to behavior.

summaries.beginner: Fly learning cells were thought to plug into smell channels at random. A detailed map shows that channels for food smells land on the same learning cells more often than chance, which a model says should make those mixtures easier to tell apart.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this study maps PN-to-Kenyon-cell synapses in an adult Drosophila whole-brain EM volume to test random-connectivity models of the mushroom body. Compared with precisely defined null models, a subset of food-responsive projection-neuron types converged on individual KCs more frequently than expected. The bias matches axon geometry: overconvergent PN types arborize near one another in the main calyx, so local KC dendrites are more likely to sample them. Computational modeling found better discrimination of input from those PN types, interpreted as an associative fovea for frequent, ethologically relevant food-odor combinations.
summaries.advanced: Rejection of pure randomness is relative to the authors’ null models; other structured nulls could remain compatible. “Food-responsive” PN types are defined from prior physiology, not from this EM animal. Discrimination advantage is simulated, not measured psychophysically. Geometric explanation (nearby arbors) may fully account for overconvergence without invoking developmental partner choice beyond axon placement.

plain_language_summary: Fly learning cells were thought to plug into smell channels at random. A detailed map shows that channels for food smells land on the same learning cells more often than chance, which a model says should make those mixtures easier to tell apart.

ocar.opportunity: Circuit models need synaptic strengths, which are costly to measure, while connectomics usually reports contact counts; if counts predicted contact area, models could use counts as a proxy.
ocar.challenge: Although synaptic surface area correlates with strength, it was unclear whether count alone predicts total synaptic area between a Drosophila neuron pair across neurotransmitters.
ocar.action: Barnes, Bonnéry, and Cardona quantified the relationship between synaptic count and synaptic area in volume EM of the larval Drosophila central nervous system.
ocar.resolution: Total synaptic surface area summed across contacts from one presynaptic neuron to a postsynaptic partner could be accurately predicted from the number of synaptic contacts alone, for a variety of neurotransmitters, supporting counts as approximations of strength when modeling circuits.
ocar.future_work: Whether the same count-to-area relationship holds in adult Drosophila and in other phyla is the caution required before using larval counts as a universal strength proxy.

summaries.beginner: Modelers often treat the number of contacts between two cells as a stand-in for connection strength. In larval fruit-fly nerve cord data, that shortcut works: more contacts predict more total contact area, for several chemical messenger types.
summaries.intermediate: This 2020 study (later PLOS ONE) measures how synaptic counts relate to synaptic contact area in larval Drosophila CNS volume EM. Although synaptic surface area is known to correlate with strength, most connectomic studies use contact counts. The authors find that total synaptic surface area summed over all contacts from one presynaptic neuron to one postsynaptic neuron can be accurately predicted from contact number alone, across a variety of neurotransmitters. They conclude that synaptic counts are a reasonable approximation of synaptic strength for circuit modeling in this system.
summaries.advanced: “Accurately predicted” is not given as an R² in the abstract. The result is larval Drosophila CNS, not a claim about mammals. Area is a structural proxy for strength, itself one step from physiology. Variety of neurotransmitters is stated without listing them here. Pairwise summed area can hide a few large versus many small synapses with the same count; the abstract says count still predicts the sum.

plain_language_summary: Modelers often treat the number of contacts between two cells as a stand-in for connection strength. In larval fruit-fly nerve cord data, that shortcut works: more contacts predict more total contact area, for several chemical messenger types.

ocar.opportunity: The mushroom body’s conserved architecture, dense connectome, and rich experimental history make it a testbed for inferring computation from synapse-level maps.
ocar.challenge: Even a completed dense MB connectome still hid unexpected visual inputs, MBON-to-descending paths, structured sensory transfer, and DAN modulation that anatomy-first analysis had to uncover.
ocar.action: Li and colleagues analyzed the adult Drosophila mushroom-body connectome, identifying new components and describing sensory input structure, MBON outputs, DAN modulation, MB–central-complex links, and feedback onto DANs.
ocar.resolution: They report extensive visual input, MBONs with direct descending-neuron connections, unexpected structure in how sensory modalities reach MBONs and how DANs modulate that transfer, plus circuitry integrating MB outputs and feeding back onto DANs. The map is offered as a foundation for theory and experiment.
ocar.future_work: The authors explicitly present the results as a foundation for further theoretical and experimental work on MB computation.

summaries.beginner: The mushroom body is the fly’s learning center. Using a detailed connection map, this paper finds more visual input than expected, output cells that talk straight to movement-related neurons, and structured ways dopamine cells gate what gets through.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2020), this study infers computation from the dense adult Drosophila mushroom-body connectome. New circuit components include extensive visual input and mushroom-body output neurons with direct connections to descending neurons. The authors describe unexpected structure in sensory inputs, in transfer of different modalities to MBONs, and in dopaminergic modulation of that transfer. They also map integration of MB outputs, connectivity with the central complex, and inputs to DANs including MBON feedback. Results are framed as a foundation for further theory and experiments on learning, memory, and activity regulation.
summaries.advanced: This eLife paper and a simultaneous bioRxiv (work_0c62223b980049c1) share nearly identical abstracts; treat them as journal versus preprint of the same analysis. “Unexpected structure” is not enumerated as statistics in the abstract. Direct MBON-to-descending connections are anatomical; whether they drive behavior is untested here. Visual input “extensive” is relative to prior MB descriptions focused on olfaction.

plain_language_summary: The mushroom body is the fly’s learning center. Using a detailed connection map, this paper finds more visual input than expected, output cells that talk straight to movement-related neurons, and structured ways dopamine cells gate what gets through.

ocar.opportunity: A dense mushroom-body connectome plus decades of learning experiments create an opportunity to infer MB computations from wiring.
ocar.challenge: Sensory mixing, MBON outputs to descending neurons, DAN modulation, and feedback onto DANs were not fully visible without synapse-level reconstruction.
ocar.action: Li and colleagues analyze the adult Drosophila MB connectome, cataloguing new components and the structure of sensory transfer and its dopaminergic modulation.
ocar.resolution: They identify extensive visual input, MBONs with direct descending connections, unexpected structure in modality transfer and DAN modulation, MB–central-complex connectivity, and MBON feedback onto DANs, as a foundation for theory and experiment.
ocar.future_work: Experimental tests of the newly highlighted visual and descending pathways are the natural follow-on from this preprint.

summaries.beginner: This preprint walks through the wiring of the fly learning center and highlights extra visual inputs and output cells that contact descending neurons. It is meant as a map for later experiments and models.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this study analyzes the adult Drosophila mushroom-body dense connectome to infer circuit computations. The authors identify new components including extensive visual input and MBONs with direct descending-neuron connections. They describe unexpected structure in sensory inputs, in transfer of information about different modalities to MBONs, and in modulation of that transfer by dopaminergic neurons. Additional results cover integration of MB outputs, MB–central-complex connectivity, and DAN inputs including MBON feedback. The preprint is a foundation for further theoretical and experimental work.
summaries.advanced: Near-duplicate of the eLife mushroom-body paper in this shard; do not treat findings as an independent replication. Abstract-level claims are qualitative (“unexpected structure,” “extensive visual input”). No numeric connection counts appear here. Implications for function remain inferential from anatomy.

plain_language_summary: This preprint walks through the wiring of the fly learning center and highlights extra visual inputs and output cells that contact descending neurons. It is meant as a map for later experiments and models.

ocar.opportunity: Mesoscale relationships between synaptic-level wiring and brain-wide functional coupling were unclear even after a fly connectome became available.
ocar.challenge: Cell- and synapse-level connectivity had not been systematically compared with whole-brain in vivo functional connectivity across the Drosophila central brain.
ocar.action: Turner, Mann, and Clandinin related the Drosophila connectome to whole-brain functional connectivity from in vivo imaging, including direct and indirect anatomical pathways and region-wise residuals.
ocar.resolution: Functional connectivity was strongly associated with the strength of both direct and indirect anatomical pathways. Mushroom body and central complex showed considerably higher functional connectivity to other regions than direct anatomy predicted. Several topological similarities with mammalian mesoscale networks suggest conserved structure–function principles.
ocar.future_work: Explaining why MB and CX are functionally overconnected relative to direct synapses—via indirect paths, neuromodulation, or imaging limitations—is the residual puzzle the authors highlight.

summaries.beginner: This paper asks whether cells that are wired together in the fly brain also tend to be active together. In general yes, including via indirect paths, but the learning and navigation centers look more functionally coupled than their direct wires suggest.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this study combines the Drosophila connectome with whole-brain in vivo imaging to relate structural and functional connectivity in the central brain. Functional connectivity is strongly associated with the strength of both direct and indirect anatomical pathways. Some regions, including the mushroom body and central complex, show considerably higher functional connectivity to other brain regions than predicted from their direct anatomical connections. The authors also report topological similarities between fly and mammalian mesoscale brain networks, suggesting conserved structure–function principles.
summaries.advanced: Functional connectivity is resting-state-style coupling from whole-brain imaging, not task-evoked responses. “Indirect anatomical pathways” can explain some coupling; MB/CX residuals indicate leftover unexplained FC. Conserved fly–mammal principles are topological analogies at mesoscale, not shared cell types. Directionality of synapses may be collapsed depending on how FC is compared to directed weights—not specified in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: This paper asks whether cells that are wired together in the fly brain also tend to be active together. In general yes, including via indirect paths, but the learning and navigation centers look more functionally coupled than their direct wires suggest.

ocar.opportunity: Large shared datasets in genomics and astronomy enable many later questions from the same resource; automated synaptic mapping now makes a similar “data-rich” approach conceivable for brain circuits.
ocar.challenge: The circuits underlying brain function are complicated, and no mouse brain has been mapped at synapse level, so the scientific return on a whole-mouse connectome remains a community argument rather than a completed fact.
ocar.action: Abbott and colleagues discuss the benefits of mapping a mouse brain at the level of synapses, analogizing to other big-science data resources.
ocar.resolution: The piece argues that mouse brain connectomics would be influential by enabling continuously arising new questions, not by answering a single question.
ocar.future_work: The commentary’s implied next step is organizing the technical and social effort required to acquire a synaptic-resolution mouse brain map.

summaries.beginner: This short Cell piece argues that mapping every connection in a mouse brain would be like the big shared catalogs in genetics and astronomy: valuable because many different questions can be asked of the same map.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Cell (2020), this commentary compares large scientific projects in genomics and astronomy—influential because they enable many new questions from the same data-rich sources—to emerging automated synaptic mapping. The authors argue that circuits underlying brain function are now ripe for analysis and discuss benefits of mapping a mouse brain at the level of synapses. The article is a perspective on why a mouse connectome would function as community infrastructure. It does not present new reconstructions.
summaries.advanced: This is opinion, with a very short abstract; there are no methods or results to caveat quantitatively. “Ripe for analysis” is a 2020 snapshot of automated mapping progress. Benefits of a mouse synaptic map are argued analogically, not demonstrated. Readers should not cite this as empirical connectomics.

plain_language_summary: This short Cell piece argues that mapping every connection in a mouse brain would be like the big shared catalogs in genetics and astronomy: valuable because many different questions can be asked of the same map.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroscientists waste effort moving among documentation, dependencies, and separate analysis/visualization environments when comparing many neurons across imaging modalities and template brains.
ocar.challenge: Most tools do not support morphology and connectivity comparison after co-registration in a common template, or transforms between templates and between light and EM.
ocar.action: Bates and colleagues developed the natverse, a suite of interoperable open-source R packages to read local and remote data, visualize and cluster neurons, perform graph analyses of branching, transform between templates, and integrate most Drosophila LM and EM connectomic datasets.
ocar.resolution: The natverse is presented as an easy environment for large-scale neuroanatomical analysis and an open platform for community packages.
ocar.future_work: Sustaining interoperability as new EM community datasets appear (beyond the Drosophila resources demonstrated) is the ecosystem’s ongoing test.

summaries.beginner: Comparing lots of fly neurons usually means fighting with many separate programs. The natverse is a set of R tools that read, plot, and match neurons in a shared brain space, including both light-microscope and electron-microscope data.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2020), this paper presents the natverse, a suite of interoperable open-source R packages for neuroanatomical data. Users can read local and remote data, visualize and cluster neurons, and run graph-theoretic analyses of neuronal branching. Unlike most tools, it supports comparison of morphology and connectivity after imaging or co-registration in a common template, and transformations between template spaces and imaging modalities. The authors demonstrate integration of the vast majority of Drosophila light-microscopy and EM connectomic datasets.
summaries.advanced: This is a software ecosystem paper; biological findings are not the unit of result. “Vast majority” of Drosophila LM and EM datasets is an integration claim as of 2020. R-centric design is a feature for that community and a barrier for Python-only labs. Template transforms inherit registration error that the abstract does not quantify.

plain_language_summary: Comparing lots of fly neurons usually means fighting with many separate programs. The natverse is a set of R tools that read, plot, and match neurons in a shared brain space, including both light-microscope and electron-microscope data.

ocar.opportunity: Whitening—decorrelating activity patterns for later classification—is a fundamental computation in the olfactory bulb, but its mechanistic implementation required a wiring diagram plus odor-evoked activity in the same animal.
ocar.challenge: Higher-order connectivity motifs adapted to natural odor patterns cannot be read from activity or incomplete anatomy alone.
ocar.action: Wanner and Friedrich measured odor-evoked activity in a zebrafish larva olfactory bulb and then reconstructed the complete wiring diagram by volumetric EM, producing a functional connectome used in simulations.
ocar.resolution: Multisynaptic motifs mediating reciprocal inhibition between similarly tuned neurons were over-represented. That connectivity suppressed redundant responses and was necessary and sufficient to reproduce whitening in simulations. Whitening is therefore attributed to higher-order wiring structure adapted to natural input patterns.
ocar.future_work: Whether the same similarly-tuned reciprocal-inhibition over-representation implements whitening in other olfactory systems is the comparative test.

summaries.beginner: The smell bulb makes odor patterns easier to tell apart by reducing overlap between them. In a young zebrafish, mapping both activity and every connection showed that cells with similar odor tastes inhibit each other in a way that performs that cleanup.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Neuroscience (2020), this study measures odor-evoked activity in a larval zebrafish olfactory bulb and then densely reconstructs its wiring diagram with volumetric EM. The functional connectome reveals an over-representation of multisynaptic motifs that mediate reciprocal inhibition between similarly tuned neurons. This connectivity suppressed redundant responses and was necessary and sufficient to reproduce whitening in simulations. The authors conclude that whitening of odor representations is mediated by higher-order structure in the wiring diagram adapted to natural input patterns.
summaries.advanced: Necessity and sufficiency are simulation results on the reconstructed circuit, not in vivo lesions of the motifs. Over-representation of specific motifs is relative to an unspecified null in the abstract. n = 1 larva for the joint activity-and-EM experiment. “Adapted to natural input patterns” is an interpretation of structure–function match, not an evolutionary measurement.

plain_language_summary: The smell bulb makes odor patterns easier to tell apart by reducing overlap between them. In a young zebrafish, mapping both activity and every connection showed that cells with similar odor tastes inhibit each other in a way that performs that cleanup.

ocar.opportunity: Cellular-level synaptic circuits for body-wide motor control in a segmented animal were largely unknown; a three-segmented Platynereis larva is small enough to reconstruct wholly.
ocar.challenge: Whole-body serial EM must be reconstructed and annotated for both neurons and non-neuronal effectors, then analyzed for modularity and intersegmental paths.
ocar.action: Verasztó and colleagues reconstructed and annotated over 1,500 neurons and 6,500 non-neuronal cells, classified 180 neuronal and 90 non-neuronal types, and traced pathways from 428 sensory neurons to ciliated cells, glands, pigment cells, and muscles.
ocar.resolution: They describe modular architecture, intersegmental cell-type differences, descending and ascending pathways, and mechanosensory and peptidergic circuits, providing a basis for understanding whole-body coordination. Somatic musculature and its innervation are deferred to a companion paper.
ocar.future_work: The companion muscle paper plus physiology of the 428-to-effector pathways would complete the structure–function account this connectome starts.

summaries.beginner: This preprint maps an entire three-segment marine worm larva: its nerve cells and many other body cells. It follows paths from hundreds of sensors to cilia, glands, pigment cells, and muscles.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020), this study presents the whole-animal synaptic connectome and cell-type complement of a three-segmented Platynereis dumerilii larva. Over 1,500 neurons and 6,500 non-neuronal cells were reconstructed and annotated; differentiated cells fall into 180 neuronal and 90 non-neuronal types. The authors analyze modular network architecture and polysynaptic pathways from 428 sensory neurons to four effector systems (ciliated cells, glands, pigment cells, and muscles). They also examine intersegmental cell-type differences, descending and ascending pathways, and mechanosensory and peptidergic circuits. Muscle innervation is reserved for a companion paper.
summaries.advanced: Counts (1,500 neurons; 6,500 non-neuronal; 180/90 types; 428 sensory neurons) are for this three-segmented larva and differ from the later 2025 whole-body paper’s larger inventory—do not merge them. One individual. Companion muscle paper means motor completeness is split. Pathway descriptions are anatomical.

plain_language_summary: This preprint maps an entire three-segment marine worm larva: its nerve cells and many other body cells. It follows paths from hundreds of sensors to cilia, glands, pigment cells, and muscles.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes of animals of the same species are architecturally similar, raising the question of where neuronal connectivity is genetically encoded.
ocar.challenge: A genetic-identity model of synapse and gap-junction formation needs falsifiable graph predictions, not only correlation with expression.
ocar.action: Barabási and Barabási hypothesize that genetic identity guides synapse and gap-junction formation, predict specific biclique motifs, and search connectomes of three species for large bicliques, then test whether neurons in those subgraphs share expression and morphology.
ocar.resolution: They identify a family of large, statistically significant biclique subgraphs. Within many bicliques, neurons share statistically significant expression patterns and morphological characteristics, consistent with common genetic drivers of synapse formation. The model offers experimentally falsifiable predictions on genetic factors for individual circuits.
ocar.future_work: The stated next step is experimental falsification: testing whether predicted genetic factors in biclique members actually drive those synapses.

summaries.beginner: Animals of one species have similar brain wiring, so genes likely help choose partners. This paper predicts a particular wiring pattern if that is true, finds those patterns in three species, and shows the cells in a pattern often share gene activity and shape.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Neuron (2019), this study starts from the hypothesis that neuronal genetic identity guides synapse and gap-junction formation and shows that such genetically driven wiring predicts biclique motifs in the connectome. The authors identify a family of large, statistically significant biclique subgraphs in connectomes of three species. Within many bicliques, neurons share statistically significant expression patterns and morphological characteristics, supporting common genetic factors. The genetic connectome model is offered as a self-consistent, experimentally falsifiable link from genetics to reproducible architecture.
summaries.advanced: Three species are not named in the abstract. Bicliques can arise from mechanisms other than shared genetic identity (e.g., shared position). Expression similarity inside bicliques is supporting evidence, not proof of developmental causation. Statistical significance of subgraphs depends on the null model. Falsifiable predictions are promised; this paper does not itself manipulate genes.

plain_language_summary: Animals of one species have similar brain wiring, so genes likely help choose partners. This paper predicts a particular wiring pattern if that is true, finds those patterns in three species, and shows the cells in a pattern often share gene activity and shape.

ocar.opportunity: EM is the gold standard for ultrastructure but has been too slow for volumes at the scale of cortical microcircuits across multiple areas.
ocar.challenge: Mapping >1 mm³ at synaptic resolution requires continuous autonomous imaging and parallelization without sacrificing section handling of tens of thousands of ultrathin sections.
ocar.action: Yin and colleagues built a parallel TEM pipeline with 24/7 autonomous imaging across six microscopes and applied it to more than 26,500 sections from one mouse neocortex block spanning four visual areas.
ocar.resolution: They acquired more than 1 mm³ at synaptic resolution in less than 6 months, producing more than 2 petabytes. Combined burst rate is 3 Gpixel/s and net rate 600 Mpixel/s with six microscopes. The work demonstrates feasibility of EM at cortical-microcircuit scale in multiple regions.
