ocar.future_work: The same parallel TEM architecture is framed as enabling datasets in multiple brain regions and species; downstream alignment and reconstruction remain the complementary bottlenecks.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes are precise but slow. This team ran six of them around the clock to photograph more than a cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex in under six months, creating over two petabytes of pictures.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Communications (2019/2020), this paper presents a petascale automated imaging pipeline using parallel transmission electron microscopes with 24/7 autonomous operation. The system imaged more than 26,500 ultrathin sections from one mouse neocortex block spanning four visual areas, acquiring more than 1 mm³ at synaptic resolution in less than 6 months and yielding more than 2 petabytes. Combined burst acquisition is 3 Gpixel per second and net rate 600 Mpixel per second with six microscopes. The authors argue this shows EM datasets at cortical-microcircuit scale are feasible across regions and species.
summaries.advanced: This is an acquisition-pipeline paper; reconstruction quality is out of scope in the abstract. Section count (>26,500) and volume (>1 mm³) are from one block. Burst versus net rates (3 vs 0.6 Gpixel/s) quantify overhead. Catalog year is 2019; the DOI is a 2020 Nature Communications article—use the row’s 2019/Nature Communications pairing as given. Alignment of cracked serial sections is the known next failure mode, not solved here.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes are precise but slow. This team ran six of them around the clock to photograph more than a cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex in under six months, creating over two petabytes of pictures.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroscience now generates some of the largest biomedical datasets, and EM connectomics is especially information-dense, so understanding its machine-learning bottleneck matters for scaling.
ocar.challenge: Current ML applications demand excessive labeled data while using only a small fraction of raw images for training, exposing a gap between artificial and biological intelligence and blocking a human nanoscale connectome.
ocar.action: Motta, Schurr, Staffler, and Helmstaedter review how data volume and analysis difficulty make EM connectomics a particularly hard big-data problem and highlight the greed for training labels.
ocar.resolution: They argue that substantial improvements in label and energy efficiency of machine learning may be required before a human nanoscale connectome is feasible.
ocar.future_work: The review’s prescribed path is more label- and energy-efficient learning, not simply more annotators, if centimetre-scale human circuits are the goal.

summaries.beginner: Brain electron-microscope projects create enormous image piles, but today’s computer tracers still need lots of hand-drawn labels. This commentary says that hunger for labels is a major reason a whole human connection map is still out of reach.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), this review compares data scale across biomedical fields and argues that EM-based connectomics is an especially hard analysis problem. As in other contemporary machine-learning applications, algorithms demand excessive labeled data while using only a small fraction of available raw images for training, illustrating a gap between artificial and biological intelligence. The authors conclude that substantial improvements in label and energy efficiency of machine learning may be required to acquire a nanoscale connectome of a human brain. The piece is a perspective on bottlenecks rather than a methods result.
summaries.advanced: Byte-scale comparisons across fields are rhetorical in the abstract, not a table. “Greed for training labels” is the central thesis; later self-supervised EM models (SegCLR, ConnectoFM, etc.) are outside this 2019 snapshot. Human nanoscale connectome feasibility is a scaling argument. Energy efficiency of ML is raised alongside label efficiency, a less common connectomics talking point.

plain_language_summary: Brain electron-microscope projects create enormous image piles, but today’s computer tracers still need lots of hand-drawn labels. This commentary says that hunger for labels is a major reason a whole human connection map is still out of reach.

ocar.opportunity: Large connectomes are arriving, promising abundant constraints for theoretical models of neural computation and tests of their predictions.
ocar.challenge: Theoretical neuroscience lacks a standard toolkit for incorporating synaptic wiring-diagram constraints into the models it usually studies, especially as datasets grow.
ocar.action: Litwin-Kumar and Turaga survey recent approaches to building models with constrained wiring diagrams and the insights those models have provided.
ocar.resolution: The article maps existing strategies and argues for new techniques to scale constrained modeling to more complex datasets.
ocar.future_work: Developing those missing standard tools—so wiring constraints can be imposed on typical theoretical models at increasing scale—is the need the review identifies.

summaries.beginner: Detailed wiring diagrams should help computer models of the brain, but theorists do not yet have a standard way to build those diagrams into their usual models. This review describes early attempts and what still needs inventing.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), this review discusses how emerging synaptic wiring diagrams can constrain computational models. The authors note that there is not yet a standard set of tools for incorporating connectomic constraints into models typically studied in theoretical neuroscience. They survey recent approaches to building models with constrained wiring diagrams and the insights obtained. They also describe challenges and the need for new techniques as datasets become more complex.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods-oriented opinion survey without new empirical results. “Standard tools” are declared missing as of 2019; later connectome-constrained networks (e.g., fly optic lobe) postdate this snapshot. Scaling challenges are identified rather than solved. The abstract does not enumerate the surveyed model classes.

plain_language_summary: Detailed wiring diagrams should help computer models of the brain, but theorists do not yet have a standard way to build those diagrams into their usual models. This review describes early attempts and what still needs inventing.
